articles.title: Marcos wants anti-political dynasty bill passed during his term
articles.summary: Marcos wants anti-political dynasty bill passed during his term

blocks.text: Published September 17, 2026 1:47pm
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. wants the anti-political dynasty bill passed within his term, according to Malacañang on Thursday.
The Supreme Court (SC) has directed Congress to enact the measure after 39 years of failing to do so. The 1987 Constitution mandates that Congress enacts a measure against political dynasties.

“Wala pa pong binabanggit na desisyon ang Supreme Court, alam na po natin na ito po ang isa sa mga priority bills ng Pangulo. Talagang ito po ay pinapamadali niya at gusto po niya hangga’t maaari sa panahon po niya ay maipasa ang anti-political dynasty law,” Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said in a media briefing.

(Even without the Supreme Court saying its decision, we know that this is one of the President’s priority bills. He is really rushing this and he wants that, as much as possible, that the anti-political dynasty law is passed during his time.)
Marcos agreed with the SC that it was time to enact a law against political dynasties, Castro said.
Castro said that Congress will decide the pace at which it passes the law but said that it was understandable that they had a lot of other pertinent work to do.
“Pero still, lumabas naman din po ang desisyon ng Supreme Court, alam din po nila, gusto din po naman nila na magkaroon po talaga ng anti-political dynasty law,” Castro said.
(But still, the Supreme Court has issued its decision, they know this, they also want there to be an anti-political dynasty law.) —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Thursday briefing: Yemen’s war continues to threaten oil supplies– but what about its people?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: The Houthi advance along the Red Sea coast raised fears for global trade and energy supplies, while more than 100,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the…

blocks.text: Good morning. The lightning advance of Houthi militants along the west coast of Yemen over the past week has prompted fears of a spiralling conflict in the region and a new oil supply crisis.

For families living in the Middle East’s poorest country, the most significant fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces in years is a crisis upon a catastrophe, with escalating civilian casualties and at least 100,000 displaced in recent days.

Houthi fighters have captured strategic islands across a critical Red Sea trade route, the Bab al-Mandab strait, one of the most important shipping routes in the world – almost 15% of global sea trade passes through it. The strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transited in peacetime, has remained largely blocked since the US and Israel launched airstrikes in February, so the prospect of Iran and its allies exerting pressure on two maritime choke points has global implications. The price of crude oil has already begun to spike.

For today’s newsletter, I spoke to Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House, about this new and dangerous dimension to the ongoing war in Yemen, and why fears over oil and global trade must not overshadow the plight of ordinary Yemenis. First, this morning’s headlines.
Five big stories

items: UK politics | Key allies of Andy Burnham have warned the prime minister not to back down over his promises to put water companies under public control, after details emerged about the prime minister’s plan to give mayors more oversight of the industry.

Environment | Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing hundreds of people in Nepal and Tibet last month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found.
Health | Women with the same medical condition as men are less likely to be offered treatment such as surgery, a stent or a strong painkiller, research has found.

Europe | The UK government’s EU reset summit will be delayed again unless the bloc agrees to discuss legislation that could lock British business out of parts of EU industry, government sources have said.
UK news | Police searching for a three-year-old boy who went missing from a playground on the Suffolk-Essex border have found a body.

blocks.text: In depth: The fight for Yemen’s Red Sea coast

blocks.caption: Yemen refugees arrive in Djibouti as intensified fighting drives displacement. Photograph: International Organization for Migration/Reuters

blocks.text: The current escalation of violence in Yemen has its roots in a civil war that broke out in 2014 between the Yemeni army and the Houthi movement, which champions Yemen’s Shia Muslim minority. A year later, the Houthis – part of Iran’s “axis of resistance”, a loose coalition of armed groups that includes Hamas and Hezbollah – toppled the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.

Al-Muslimi grew up in a remote mountain village in Yemen, where his family made honey, one of the country’s most lucrative and popular exports. His mother used to tease him because the bees didn’t recognise him after he spent long periods studying away from home – he was the only person in his family who had to wear a beekeeping suit.

Al-Muslimi now writes about how the years-long internecine conflict has had a devastating impact on the honey trade and the farmers who tend Yemeni bees. At least 150,000 people have been killed since 2014, mainly through aerial bombardment by the Saudi-backed coalition that supports the Yemeni government, which has resumed this week. About 4.5 million people – the population of Birmingham and Greater Manchester combined – have already been displaced by fighting over the past decade, while the UN estimates that more than 18.2 million – twice the population of London – are in dire need of humanitarian assistance.

The situation now is “worse than 2015”, says Al-Muslimi, with global attention diverted to crises in Syria, Sudan, and Ukraine and now focused on oil prices and regional consequences. “There is even less willingness to help civilians.”

After the Houthis captured the port city of Mocha, birthplace of the global coffee trade, last week, Al-Muslimi heard local media reports of more than 240 pregnant women ready to give birth without accessible healthcare.
“It’s absolutely nuts,” he says. “This is a country that was already suffering so many things, including indifference.”
How has the conflict escalated in the past week?

It has been plain for months to Yemen-watchers that the Houthis were preparing for a significant offensive, says al-Muslimi. This erupted about a week ago with the militants seizing control of parts of the west coast and gaining a hold over the Bab al-Mandab strait, including the strategic port of Mocha and key islands of Perim, Greater and Lesser Hanish in the 20-mile stretch of water that forms a natural chokepoint on the trade route connecting Asia with Europe.

With government supporters in disarray, the degree of division among anti-Houthi forces is complicating the fight back. The Houthis have achieved what Al-Muslimi calls “the most consequential change in territorial control in Yemen for years”.

Since then, the Houthis have claimed responsibility for missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, including the bombing of a critical east-west oil pipeline. On Wednesday a military spokesperson for the Houthis denied attempting to fly a drone close to the holy city of Mecca, and claimed that Saudi Arabia has carried out as many as 450 airstrikes in Yemen ‌this week in retaliation. The ongoing aggression is driving fears that more Muslim nations could be drawn into the conflict.
What does it mean for global oil supply?

If ​the Houthis were to close the Bab al-Mandab strait, vessels would be forced to reroute all the way around the southern tip of Africa. The consequences for the global economy could be dire, particularly when taken along with the ongoing blockade of Hormuz.

With Iran and its Houthi allies controlling potentially a third of energy trade globally, “it’s more dangerous than a nuclear bomb,” says Al-Muslimi bluntly, “especially at a time when the world still depends massively on this type of energy”.

Attacks on Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline – which is now closed for repairs and has been crucial for moving oil from the strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea export hub of Yanbu – will add further pressure to global supplies.

Al-Muslimi advises caution over Houthi claims that they don’t intend to impose transit fees on vessels passing through Bab al-Mandab. The UN security council has seen evidence that, since the militants started attacks on Red Sea shipping in 2023, in response to Israel’s decimation of Gaza, the Houthis have been extracting informal payments from some shipping agencies in return for safe passage.

Meanwhile, Saudi anger with Iran for assisting Houthi attacks saw the cancellation of a meeting with Gulf states about the future of the strait of Hormuz on Monday. Reports in the early hours today that Saudi Arabia may be offering more crude cargoes through Oman saw the price of Brent crude drop to $104.59 a barrel after hitting $108 earlier this week. But for perspective, it was trading at $80 a barrel in early July.

This comes as the average price of diesel in the US hit $6 per gallon for the first time last week, with the Iran war, combined with Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, continuing to squeeze supply.
What does it mean for the region?

The UN security council held an emergency meeting in New York on Tuesday to discuss the escalating violence in Yemen and threats to maritime security, with members urging maximum restraint to avoid the situation devolving into a wider regional war. The conflict is the first test of a mutual defence pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, announced in August – but Saudi has yet to publicly call on either for assistance.

Meanwhile, Al-Muslimi says the US, a close Saudi ally, faces a dilemma. The States reached a truce with the Houthis in May 2025, after conducting airstrikes against the group after attacks on Red Sea shipping. “The existing truce gives both sides reasons for restraint,” he says. “For Trump, preserving that arrangement helps keep the US away from another costly Middle Eastern military confrontation while it remains engaged in the strait of Hormuz. The Houthis have equally strong incentives to not be drawn into conflict with the US, which caused them serious damage in the 2025 bombing campaign.”

Yesterday the Guardian confirmed that officials from the US had met Houthi leaders over the weekend in Oman, where they received assurances that the ceasefire still held and that the movement had no intention of attacking US shipping in the Red Sea. While Trump condemned the Houthi advance for threatening freedom of navigation, he has far rejected any military response in support of Riyadh.

Al-Muslimi calls for a more coherent international approach to his country, which he considers one of the least understood in the region. Yemen analysts have frequently criticised the US and allies for approaching Yemen’s challenges with a focus on security rather than diplomacy or development, while internal instability has been exploited by larger regional powers to fight their own proxy battles.

Most importantly, he says: “While this new international dimension of Yemen’s war makes the country strategically more important to the world, it should not overshadow the plight of ordinary Yemenis”.

articles.title: Marcoleta solicited campaign donation from co-accused in plunder raps --witness
articles.summary: Marcoleta solicited campaign donation from co-accused in plunder raps --witness

blocks.text: Published September 17, 2026 1:38pm
Senator Rodante Marcoleta solicited campaign donations from his friend, businessman Aristotle Viray, a witness from the Office of the Ombudsman told the Sandiganbayan Third Division on Thursday.

Field Investigation Bureau Director Maria Melinda Mananghaya-Henson of the Office of the Ombudsman made the testimony during the hearing on the bail petition filed by Marcoleta, Viray and their two other co-accused, former Anakalusugan party-list Rep. Michael Defensor and Joseph Espiritu involving a P75 million plunder case filed against them over Marcoleta's undeclared campaign donation worth P75 million.

"It was accused Marcoleta who actually solicited [the donation]," Henson said when asked by Sandiganbayan Third Division chairperson Karl Miranda about the defense of Viray as stated in the latter's counter affidavit submitted before the Ombudsman.

Henson earlier testified that part of the donor’s tax for the P75 million campaign donation for Marcoleta given by Viray, Espiritu and Defensor was paid by Ebenezer Santos, who is an employee of Marcoleta.

Likewise, Henson said that Marcoleta and his co-accused were in collusion, given that the Deeds of Donation of the Donors were all made and notarized belatedly in November 2025 even if the donation was already made in January 2025.

Based on the criminal information filed by the Ombudsman prosecutors, the donor’s tax for the said P75 million campaign donation was only paid in December 2025, an indication of concealment since the donation was already made in January 2025.

Marcoleta, in a television interview in November 2025, said that he received such P75 million donation from his friends but he did not declare this as campaign expenditure because it was upon the request of the donors to become anonymous.
The Senator, however, said in his position paper submitted to the Commission on Elections (Comelec) that such donation was a personal fund of his, prompting the Comelec to stop the investigation.
This difference in Marcoleta’s accounts was included in the basis of the Ombudsman’s probe and eventual filing of charges against Marcoleta and his co-accused. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: DOJ on Robin Padilla feeling 'discriminated:' We are duty bound to act on complaints
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) said Thursday that it is duty-bound to act on complaints filed with the agency, following Senator Robin Padilla"s remarks that he felt “discriminated” against over his…

blocks.text: Published September 17, 2026 1:37pm

The Department of Justice (DOJ) said Thursday that it is duty-bound to act on complaints filed with the agency, following Senator Robin Padilla’s remarks that he felt “discriminated” against over his obstruction of justice case.

“Were duty-bound, as soon as we receive any complaint to request any respondent to appear before us to submit their counteraffidavits and their supporting evidence via a subpoena,” Justice Undersecretary Ian Norman Dato said at a press briefing.

Last week, the DOJ issued a subpoena for Padilla in connection to his obstruction of justice complaint over Senator Ronald Bato dela Rosa’s departure from the Senate premises amid an International Criminal Court (ICC) warrant against him.
Padila, after receiving the subpoeba, said he felt discriminated against as the case stemmed from an international arrest warrant.
He said that the government should just bring the case to the tribunal.
Dato, meanwhile, stressed that the subpoena is not a finding of guilt but an opportunity to give respondents the opportunity to be heard.

“The issuance of a subpoena is not a finding of guilt. This is the preliminary investigaiton stage where respondents are given the full opportunity to answer the allegations before any finding of a prima facie case is made,” he said.
The DOJ directed Padilla to appear before the panel of prosecutors and to submit his counter-affidavit on September 25, Friday, and October 9, Friday.
Dato warned that a failure to appear will be considered a waiver to the respondets’ right to heard.
“Failure to appear will be considered a waiver of the right to defense and the case will be resolved based on the evidence on record,” he said.
He assured that the complaint will be resolved based on evidence and the law.
Meanwhile, Padilla maintained that he did not help Dela Rosa escape and that his colleague only hitched a ride in his car. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: The Villafuertes of CamSur: A tale of political survival and reinvention
articles.summary: The Villafuertes have figured in well-publicized teleserye-like dramas: from family feuds, celebrity marriages, social media tit for tat, to political wranglings, reinvention, and shifting political…

blocks.text: Editor’s note: This is part of a Rappler series on Filipino families that have held political power for generations. The series traces how they built their influence, where it is strongest, and how it has endured over time. Each profile examines family ties, political networks, business interests, and roles in local and national government.
For nearly 40 years, the Villafuertes have kept a generational grip on Camarines Sur (CamSur) in Bicol.

“Ever since I was a child, the Villafuertes have been in control of CamSur, and now that I have a child of my own, they are still the ones in control,” said 28-year-old CamSur voter Adela, who chose not to reveal her real name.
This familiarity is not only because they rule the province. Buildings in their barangay and even relief goods during calamities would bear the family’s name, Adela recalled.
To many residents, CamSur is essentially a “Villafuerte province.”

It is also because clan members constantly make headlines. Over the years, they have figured in well-publicized teleserye-like dramas: from family feuds, celebrity marriages, to political wranglings, and shifting political alliances.

blocks.caption: FATHER-SON. Camarines Sur Governor Luigi Villafuerte (left) with his father Camarines Sur 2nd District Representative LRay Villafuerte (center) at the groundbreaking of the new CamSur Manufacturing hub in February 2025. Photo from Luigi Villafuerte’s Facebook

blocks.text: In the 2025 midterm local elections, the dynasty easily maintained its political dominance in the province. For the top executive post, family patriarch LRay Villafuerte reclaimed the gubernatorial seat.
It was definitely a closer fight than what they were used to, but he still beat Bong Rodriguez with a 93,032-vote lead after dominating the polls across four of five districts.
In District 5, his son Migz Villafuerte also swept the vote. Younger brother Luigi Villafuerte also secured a resounding victory in the 2nd District.

The political playing field in the province is so heavily tilted in the favor of the clan, that it would be difficult for anyone to challenge their machine, explained Mary Joyce Bulao, a researcher specializing in local politics. Bulao is also former lecturer and chairperson of the Social Sciences Department at Ateneo de Naga University.
“Villafuerte is at the center and at the top, they have been operating as a provincial political machine, maintaining a structured, hierarchical organization,” Bulao explained in Filipino.

This includes control over municipal mayors, she pointed out in an interview with Rappler. If a mayor is not aligned with them, Bulao said, it typically politicizes the distribution of resources and affects the development of the area.

blocks.caption: DYNASTY. CamSur 2nd District Representative LRay Villafuerte (right) takes a photo with fellow politicians, including the President’s son, Ilocos Representative Sandro Marcos, his two sons CamSur Governor Luigi Villafuerte (middle), 5th District Representative Migz Villafuerte (second from the le…

blocks.text: It all began with Mariano Villafuerte, an orator who served two terms as congressman and became governor in 1942.
Mariano’s son, Luis Sr., who was also known as “gurang” or “old man” in Bikol, governed the province for 15 years across separate terms from 1986 to 1992 and 1995 to 2004.

The senior Luis, who was born in Naga City, used to serve as a Batasang Pambansa assemblyman and trade minister under the late president Ferdinand E. Marcos. However, by 1984 — before the 1986 EDSA People Power Revolution ousted the Marcos regime — he already shifted to the opposition.

Saysay Bikol — a civic organization of historians, educators, and cultural heritage advocates based in Naga City — described Luis Sr.’s political career as possessing “adaptability and patronage” that could “secure long-term power across shifting regimes.”
Under Corazon Aquino’s presidency, Luis Sr. became the secretary of government reorganization. He eventually served as governor of CamSur, initially from 1986–1992 and then from 1995 to 2004.
When he reached his three-term limit in 2004, he vied for and was elected representative of the 2nd District of Camarines Sur, which originally included Naga City.

blocks.caption: FATHER AND SON. Former CamSur Governor Luis Villafuerte Sr. (left) and his son, LRay Villafuerte (right), pose for a photo. Photo courtesy of LRay Villafuerte’s Facebook page.

blocks.text: The senior Luis initially encouraged his nephew, the late DILG secretary and Naga City mayor Jesse Robredo, to enter politics in 1989. But the two eventually had a bitter falling out.

In 1998, his son Luis Raymund (LRay) challenged Robredo for Naga City mayor but lost the contest. LRay eventually vied for the gubernatorial seat. He won and served in this capacity from 2004 to 2010.

Meanwhile, as district representative, Luis Sr. authored House Bill No. 4231 in the 14th Congress prior to the 2010 elections. This resulted in Republic Act No. 9716, which consolidated the municipalities of Libmanan, Minalabac, Pamplona, Pasacao, and San Fernando from the old 1st District with the towns of Gainza and Milaor from the previous 2nd District to create a new 2nd District.
The law increased the province’s districts from four to five.

It was a matter of political exigency. The 1st District was traditionally the domain of the Andaya clan. At the time the law was enacted, then-president Arroyo’s son, Dato Arroyo, was representing the 1st District. Andaya, who served as budget secretary under the Arroyo administration, was set to reclaim the seat.
Arroyo eventually vied for the newly-constituted 2nd District while Luis Sr. was elected congressman of the newly-formed 3rd District.

In the election that followed (2013), LRay ran for the second district, which was created by the law that his father authored. He lost to Dato Arroyo. His mother, Nelly Favis Villafuerte, vied for the same post for the third district also in 2013, and lost to Leni Robredo.
That marked the end of the Villafuerte family’s hold on the 3rd District.
Luis Sr. attempted to reclaim the seat in both the 2016 and 2019 elections, but lost both times to Gabriel Bordado Jr.
After serving three consecutive terms as governor, LRay also managed to secure the 2nd District in 2016, succeeding Dato Arroyo.

After LRay reached his term limit as governor in 2013, his son, Miguel Luis or Migz, entered the scene, taking over from 2013 to 2022. When Migz hit his term limit in 2022, Luigi succeeded him from 2022 to 2025.

By 2025, with their father LRay hitting his own three-term cap in the House, Luigi stepped down from the governorship to run for LRay’s congressional seat. This allowed his father to reclaim the gubernatorial seat and complete a seamless family relay in the political scene.

blocks.caption: POGING SERBIDOR? Villafuerte supporters wave a poster displaying the family trio with the text ‘Poging serbidor tunay na maaasahan’ in 2022. Photo courtesy of LRay Villafuerte’s Facebook page

blocks.text: In the 2013 elections, members of the family figured in a high profile internal feud. Luis Sr. ran directly against his grandson, Migz, in the gubernatorial race.
Mirroring the political survival and alliance-shifting that defined his career, Luis Sr. broke away from his family and teamed up with other influential local political families.
Many locals suspected that the public fight was merely staged. After all, no matter who turned against whom, the position remained safely in the hands of their dynasty.
Beyond family drama, the brothers Migz and Luigi actively pursued controversy, celebrity, and high-profile relationships.
LRay himself has figured in numerous viral social media spats.

The book Patronage Democracy in the Philippines: Clans, Clients, and Competition in Local Elections noted that topless pictures of Migz used to circulate online, aiding his popularity among young voters.
His high profile courtship of singer-actress Sarah Geronimo — while he was still serving as CamSur governor — was the subject of gossip columns from 2011 to 2013.
Migz eventually married Miss Universe Philippines 2017 Rachel Peters.
His brother Luigi also recently became engaged to actress Yassi Pressman, who previously endorsed the clan-linked Bicol Saro partylist.

blocks.caption: INFRASTRUCTURE MARK. A waiting shed bearing the name of LRay Villafuerte stands along a road in Canaman, Camarines Sur. Photo by Lyndee Buenagua

blocks.text: The Villafuertes are also known for actively shaping their own narratives.
LRay, in particular, frequently uses Facebook to defend the clan against criticism.

The Villafuertes also often prioritize highly visible developmental agendas where they can imprint their names, Bulao noted. “Kasi ‘pag nakikita ng tao, tatatak ‘yon, mas mabilis.” (When people see it, they remember, it’s much faster.)

Throughout the province, numerous projects and public buildings bear the dynasty’s name or distinct symbols. For voters like Adela, this is often all it takes. She explained how Luis Sr. made it possible for her barangay’s basketball court to be covered.

Furthermore, a sports complex in Pili is called “Ka Fuerte,” which connects to the family brand: “Serbisyong Ka Fuerte.” The same brand is reiterated in public services such as healthcare assistance programs, mobile clinics, and educational scholarships.
In 2024, during the onslaught of Typhoon Kristine, LRay and Migz were also documented distributing cash directly to residents while navigating flooded areas by boat.

It is a projection of power, Bulao noted. The message is: “Andito ako para tulungan kayo. Ako ‘yong malaking tao na tutulong sa maliit na tao.” (“I am here to help you.” I am the powerful man helping the poor.)
Whether or not that help is the one they need is beside the point. – with reports from Gemma Mendoza/Rappler.com

At a press briefing, PNP spokesperson Police Colonel Allen Rae Co said authorities continue to search for individuals who have outstanding warrants of arrest.

Co was responding to a question about the Bureau of Immigration's confirmation that one of Romualdez's co-accused had managed to leave the Philippines.

The BI said that Joselyn Serenio departed from the country prior to the issuance of a hold departure order (HDO) against her and the other respondents.

articles.title: International students, 'visa hoppers' and backpackers targeted in Australia migration crackdown
articles.summary: The government wants to reduce net overseas migration to 225,000 people by 2028.

blocks.text: International students, so-called "visa hoppers" and backpackers will be targeted under stricter rules announced by Australia on Thursday in a bid to curb immigration.
Foreign students will no longer be able to bring their families with them and those who want to extend their stay must choose a higher qualification.

Rules will also be stricter for working holiday visas - commonly used by backpackers and a crucial labour source for the agricultural sector - with a ballot system although these changes will not affect the UK.
The new rules were revealed by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke who said that while immigration was a "strength" of Australia, there needed to be a "high level of control".
For international student and graduate visas, Burke said: "We will no longer be adding to the stock of students automatically being able to bring family members over."
There would be exemptions for foreign students already in Australia as well as applicants from the Pacific and South East Asian countries, he said.
PhD students would also be able to bring their families as they were in different life circumstances to undergraduates, Burke said.

In a speech titled "The work of managing the migration program: who arrives, who stays, who leaves", Burke revealed a raft of changes as the government aims to bring net overseas migration to 225,000 people by 2028.

On student visas, he said the government would clamp down on "visa hopping" - where a student finishes a course, then applies to do another course which is often a lower qualification and sometimes with a "not so legitimate provider".
Students who want to go "up the scale" will be allowed, Burke said, for example, if a student finishes a bachelor's degree and then wants to complete a masters.
He also announced major changes to working holiday visas for those aged 18 to 30 years old who can work in Australia for 12 months, but can extend for a second and third year.
Currently, these visa holders must work for three months in regional Australia during their first year to qualify for a second year, and then six months to qualify for a third year.
Under the new changes, those who qualify for a second year will have to go into a ballot with a cap of 45,000, down from the 57,000 who qualified last year.

For the third year, the ballot will be limited to 5,000, down from 31,000 who qualified last year. British working holidaymakers will not be affected by these changes due to the UK's free trade agreement with Australia.
New figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday showed Australia's population grew 1.4% in the 12 months to March 2026 to 27.9m.
That total figure included births and deaths as well as a net overseas migration of 292,100.
Migration remains a major political issue as debate around Australia's population grows amid rising living costs, housing affordability and increased strain on public services.

One Nation, a populist right-wing party known for its anti-immigration stance and which has seen a surge in support in recent months, detailed its migration policy earlier this week, proposing to cut temporary migrant visas by 750,000 over three years.

The party, which won its first lower house seat in May, also wants to cap net overseas immigration to 130,000, drawing a rebuke from Burke who said such a proposal would risk "smashing parts of the Australian economy".
In July, the government introduced a policy to prioritise applications for family visas lodged onshore - where the applicant is in the country already - over those submitted overseas.
Skilled migrants already in Australia who applied for permanent visas were also prioritised over those applying from overseas.
It also paused applications for working holiday visas from 24 countries, not including the UK.

Violet Roumeliotis, from Settlement Services International which helps new arrivals to Australia, says the migration debate was increasingly driven by "short-term politics rather than what is best for the country".
"The proposed changes to family visas for international students is a good example of this," she said, adding that it would make it harder for Australia to compete for "future talent".

articles.title: Women in England with incurable breast cancer to get life-extending drug on NHS
articles.summary:
Thousands with HER2-low advanced breast cancer will have access to Enhertu after ministers strike deal on price

Thousands of women in England with incurable breast cancer will get access to…

blocks.text: Thousands of women in England with incurable breast cancer will get access to a life-extending drug on the NHS after negotiations over its cost proved successful.
About 1,000 women a year with HER2-low advanced breast cancer will be able to obtain Enhertu from Thursday after ministers and the drug’s makers struck a deal on its price.
About one in seven of the 60,000 new cases of breast cancer diagnosed every year in the UK are HER2-positive.

Clinical trials have shown that Enhertu almost doubled median progression-free survival compared with normal chemotherapy, from 5.1 months to 9.9 months. Median overall survival among people who used it was 23.4 months, compared with 16.8 months among those not on it – a 6.6-month gain.

“This is a momentous day for thousands of people who will now have access to a drug that will give them the opportunity to gain precious time with loved ones”, said Claire Rowney, the chief executive of Breast Cancer Now.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) announced on Thursday that about 1,000 patients a year in England will be eligible to receive the treatment from the NHS after it recommended it for routine use.
Nice, which advises the NHS on whether treatments represent value for money, had previously rejected Enhertu, in July 2024, as too expensive to justify, despite its proven effectiveness.
Rowney hailed “this milestone victory”, which follows two years of determined campaigning by the charity, cancer specialists and women with that form of breast cancer.

The drug has been available since December 2023 in Scotland, which is one of 27 European countries that provide it to patients. Labour ministers, including ex-health secretary Wes Streeting, have been working behind the scenes for some time to add England to that list by brokering a deal on cost. Their efforts were hampered by the drugmakers’ refusal to lower their price.

Nice’s U-turn follows recent renewed negotiations between it, NHS England and Enhertu’s two makers, the pharmaceutical firms AstraZeneca and Daiichi Sankyo. They resulted in what Nice called “a commercial solution” that means the drug is now available in England for the first time.
after newsletter promotion

The freedom that Nice gained in April to recommend that the NHS can spend up to £35,000 a year on a patient’s treatment, up from a previous maximum of £30,000, proved crucial. It has agreed to pay more for Enhertu than it was previously prepared to do. But it is unclear if the drug’s two makers reciprocated by reducing the amount they had been seeking.

“This is hugely positive news for women with secondary breast cancer who will now be offered this life-extending treatment on the NHS,” said Dr Anne Rigg, a consultant medical oncologist who is also NHS England’s national speciality adviser for chemotherapy.
Dr Catherine Elliott, Cancer Research UK’s director of research, said: “Enhertu is a targeted treatment that delivers chemotherapy directly to cancer cells.

“Clinical trial results show that, for people with HER2-low advanced breast cancer whose disease has progressed following treatment, it can help them live longer and delay their cancer from getting worse compared with standard chemotherapy.”
Ministers in Wales and Northern Ireland are likely to implement Nice’s recommendation and make it available there too.
Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said: “Enhertu can be life-changing and this recommendation means NHS patients will finally be able to benefit from it.

“It is a tribute to the campaigners and charities who never stopped pressing for this, and it follows the changes this government has made to the Nice framework as part of the UK-US pharmaceutical partnership so more people can benefit from cutting-edge treatments.”

articles.title: Rosenberg: Russia's elections will have few surprises, but for the Kremlin they matter
articles.summary: There is no doubt over the outcome of this vote, but for the Kremlin they are still an important moment.

blocks.text: Low expectations that Russia's election will bring peace closer, Steve Rosenberg reports
BySteve Rosenberg
Russia editorReporting fromMoscow and Dmitrov
The system of power in Russia is often referred to as "managed democracy" (where the Kremlin does the managing).
That means huge powers for the president and few political surprises.
This weekend's election is set to deliver another parliament dominated by the party of power, United Russia, and a house of MPs fiercely loyal to Vladimir Putin.
Critics dismiss the vote as neither free nor fair.
But the Kremlin doesn't care what the critics say.
"We have our own political system, our own political process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov explained recently.
That means no curveballs for the Kremlin. No surprises. So no story?
Far from it.
For the Kremlin, the election of 450 deputies to the lower house of parliament, the Duma, is important. This is the first parliamentary election here since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Kremlin will use it to claim that most Russians back the president and the war, as well as to promote the political careers of soldiers back from Ukraine: officials say nearly two hundred war veterans are taking part in the election.

blocks.caption: Image caption, This election is being used to promote the political careers of some military veterans

blocks.text: This election is being used to promote the political careers of some military veterans
As for the election campaign, that has provided a window on Russian society four-and-a-half years into the war.
I said no surprises. But there have been some.
"Good evening and welcome to tonight's campaign speeches by candidates for Duma Electoral District 158," said the anchor on state TV.
The studio director cut to a wide shot revealing six empty lecterns.
"The candidates haven't turned up," admitted the host. "So, it's goodbye from me."
In another TV debate (where the politicians were present) one crooning candidate sang his pitch:
"The Communist Party, onwards we go!
"We're with the people, don't you know?"
More X Factor than exit poll.

Yet a musical manifesto is strangely appropriate. In the previous Duma, everyone seemed to be singing from the same hymn sheet. At the final session of parliament in July, MPs stood and applauded as the speaker of the house chanted repeatedly:
"Russia, Putin, Victory! Russia, Putin, Victory!"
It was a signal that all MPs in parliament should back President Putin and the war.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov [centre] backs the war in Ukraine

blocks.text: Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov [centre] backs the war in Ukraine

"All parties in the Duma, every single one, voted in favour of 170 laws to support the special military operation," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told me with obvious pride about the last parliament.
"In that sense there is 100% agreement in the Duma."

I caught up with Zyuganov on the campaign trail outside Moscow at a bread and biscuit factory. As I watched rows of identical-looking loaves speeding along the conveyer I thought about Russia's parliament. It's not that all parties in the Duma are identical: some are more nationalist, others – like Zyuganov's party - more left-wing.

But when it comes to backing the Kremlin's legislative initiatives and supporting the "special military operation" they vote the same way. Such "systemic" parties are vital cogs in Russia's Kremlin-centric political machine.
And if a party doesn't support the war?

One such party - Yabloko - is calling for a ceasefire in Ukraine. Back in July it was the only anti-war party in Russia to be registered for the election. Twelve days later, though, the Supreme Court removed it from the ballot. That was widely interpreted as a sign of Kremlin concern that anti-war messaging could strike a chord with Russian voters.

Despite Yabloko's exclusion from the party list, some of its candidates are still running in individual constituency races. Though in recent weeks growing numbers of Yabloko candidates have been detained by police, prosecuted for various offences and barred from the election.
"The police are carrying out a political order. That's no secret," Yabloko candidate Grigory Grishin tells me.
"This way, the authorities are setting the boundaries within which they believe the elections should take place.

"It is well known that the demand for an end to the bloodshed in this conflict with Ukraine is very popular. In my opinion, most people in Russia now want peace and Yabloko helped people express this. That's why it's been excluded from the party lists, and why individual candidates are being barred."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Grigory Grishin says he believes demand for an end to the bloodshed in the conflict with Ukraine is very popular

blocks.text: Grigory Grishin says he believes demand for an end to the bloodshed in the conflict with Ukraine is very popular
For now, Grigory remains a candidate. But the police recently came to his flat.

"Three policemen in civilian clothes asked me to accompany them to the station, which I did. The police said I had posted what they claimed was an extremist symbol: the word 'Navalny' and that, by doing so, I had propagandised extremism via my Telegram channel."
Alexei Navalny was Russia's most prominent opposition leader and Kremlin critic who died in prison in 2024. He'd been convicted on several charges, including extremism.

The Russian authorities insist that the Duma elections are transparent and fair. Critics of the vote point to opposition politicians who have been forced into exile or put in prison. Last year one of the leaders of a prominent independent election monitoring group in Russia was jailed for five years. Grigory Melkonyants was convicted on charges of working with an "undesirable organisation". His election monitoring group, Golos, has shut down.
Fifty miles from Moscow, in the town of Dmitrov, I see little sign of an election.
In the town centre there's a memorial to "Heroes of the special military operation": local people killed fighting in Ukraine.
The war is front and centre of people's minds here.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Olga's son-in-law is fighting in Russia's "special military operation"

blocks.text: Olga's son-in-law is fighting in Russia's "special military operation"

"We feel it," says Olga, whose son-in-law is a soldier in the "special operation". "Because of the people who've gone to fight and the families left behind with sons, husbands, children and grandchildren there. But these elections can't influence what will happen."
"I'd like us to live in a peaceful country, with no war," Polina tells me, "So that you don't have to worry that a drone will fall down in front of you."
Russians have other concerns, too. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries have sparked widespread fuel shortages, while economic pressures are increasing.

"What worries me," says a barber called Ivan, "is that no matter how much you earn it's not enough. Prices are rising faster than wages. I speak to lots of people in my job. I know how hard-up they are."
Expectations are low that this election will change much.

"Western elections and elections in Russia are completely different things," Grishin explains. "Elections in the West are a way of forming a government, which is replaced later if voters aren't satisfied.

"Elections in Russia never bring a change in government. At best, they're a way of influencing it, of sending a signal. But power in Russia never changed because of an election. That's how Russia is."

articles.title: Assad regime planned US journalist's kidnap for weeks, BBC finds
articles.summary: Austin Tice’s abduction was approved by Syria’s former leader Bashar al-Assad, a source claims.

blocks.text: US journalist Austin Tice, who disappeared in Syria in 2012, was kidnapped in a calculated operation which was more than a month in the planning, the BBC can reveal.
A member of the group which detained Tice has also claimed the abduction was sanctioned by Syria's leader at the time, President Bashar al-Assad.

Tice was seen getting into a car with a driver he knew and trusted. For years, many assumed they had stumbled upon a government checkpoint, and that the abduction of the journalist had been opportunistic.
But we have uncovered evidence that, in fact, his disappearance was anything but chance.

In a new BBC podcast: Where is Austin Tice? Series 3 of I'm Not A Monster Presents, we reveal the findings of a years-long investigation into what happened to Tice, who had been reporting on Syria's civil war at the time.
His case has been followed closely by international media and cited by successive US presidents.
Georgetown University law student Tice, who had served as a US Marines captain, was last seen in a video - blindfolded and in apparent distress - posted more than a month after his capture.
As the regime fell 12 years later, tens of thousands of people emerged from the administration's prisons. Tice was not one of them.
We obtained co-ordinates from an intelligence source for multiple locations US authorities suspected he could have been held at, and searched for him for more than a month, but found no sign of him.
A former Syrian commander has said Tice was executed. Others have questioned this account and no remains have been found.

But in the aftermath of the regime's collapse, we did uncover secret Syrian intelligence files on Tice - hundreds of pages of internal records providing the first definitive proof that it was the regime that had held the journalist.
Two crucial questions remained unanswered, however: how exactly had Tice been taken in the first place? And, who was responsible for his abduction?

We have spoken to a number of men from the regime involved in Tice's detention, and have reviewed recordings of discussions about it. One man we spoke to, Abu Ali, is a former member of the National Defence Forces (NDF), a militia which was fiercely loyal to Assad.

He says the abduction operation began when Tice's driver - who multiple sources say had been passing the regime information for some time - told a senior NDF member that Tice was moving through rebel-held areas, reporting on the opposition.

Tice had pushed into areas most journalists deemed too dangerous and was writing front-page stories for the Washington Post. The Assad regime was cracking down on anyone highlighting its human rights abuses.

We have been told the NDF member Tice's driver spoke to was Sakr Rustom - not just any NDF militia contact, but nephew of Bassam al-Hassan, one of Assad's most trusted security figures and head of the NDF.
The information on Tice was passed up to Hassan, Abu Ali says, who is then said to have telephoned Assad.
"Bring him to us," Assad replied, claims Abu Ali.
Abu Ali says he was subsequently called into Hassan's office and told the president had approved the operation.
But Tice was not taken immediately. The driver, Abu Ali says, suggested that he and the NDF continue watching him, to uncover more about what he was doing.
"He trusts me," Abu Ali recalls the driver saying.
Some time later, the driver reported back that Tice's actions seemed suspicious, Abu Ali says.
Tice, as a trained marine, would sometimes share his military experience with rebel fighters - according to several people we spoke to - and would correct fighters on how they used their weapons.

To the men watching him, that behaviour made Tice look less like a journalist and more like someone from the CIA. The BBC has found no evidence to suggest this was the case, and a former senior US official responsible for part of Tice's case has denied he was an intelligence officer.

In the days before Tice vanished, the driver made one particularly brazen move while Tice was interviewing rebel fighters. He secretly took the American's backpack, containing his MacBook, a satellite transmitter and other personal items, for regime operatives to look through, multiple sources say.

On 11 August 2012, Tice celebrated his 31st birthday at a rebel safehouse on the western edge of Damascus, a few miles from Assad's presidential palace. There was a swimming pool, Free Syrian Army fighters, Taylor Swift music and whiskey, Tice revealed in what would become his final tweet.
"Hands down, best birthday ever," he wrote.
Then came the time for Tice to leave Syria. He had told various people he was planning to take time out in Lebanon.

But he was not heading to safety. He was heading to a state facility where Hassan had an office, in an area called Tahouneh on the outskirts of Damascus, according to several sources. Abu Ali was waiting there for Tice.
Abu Ali says Tice's driver told him that when he drew up to the gates, he pulled out a gun.

Tice laughed at first, Ali recalls the driver saying, apparently believing the man he trusted was joking. But the driver told Tice he was serious, Abu Ali says, and the journalist realised what was happening.
According to Ali, Tice pulled out his chequebook and pleaded with the driver to name his price, rather than go through with the kidnap.
NDF militia members then grabbed Tice, covering his eyes, Abu Ali says.
Another NDF member told us he would never forget Tice's expression as he realised he had been betrayed. Abu Ali says Hassan immediately called President Assad to tell him they had the American.
For years, the identity of Tice's driver has remained a mystery.
The BBC spoke to more than 20 people to discover who he was, with the trail eventually leading to the city of Homs, and the family of a man called Hamid Abu Obeid.
They confirmed he was the man who had driven Tice away, an account also supported by multiple NDF members. But by the time we identified him, Abu Obeid had disappeared.
His family say they do not know where he is, and fear for his safety. They say they were not aware of Hamid's involvement in Tice's case, and learned about it from him afterwards.
But they did give a motive for his betrayal of Tice.
The Abu Obeid family, Palestinian refugees from Gaza, live in poverty. Under Syrian law they are not entitled to Syrian citizenship and live under significant restrictions.

According to Hamid's brother, he had been promised a passport, Syrian citizenship, a house, and a weapon, in return for delivering Tice - life-changing rewards. But after the abduction, the family says all he got was a pistol.

Then, after Assad's regime fell, Abu Obeid's wife says her husband was called by a man who knew about his involvement in Tice's case and was threatening to tell the US embassy, hoping it might help him secure asylum.

Abu Obeid urged him not to. He then took some money, told his wife he was going shopping, and she says she has not seen him since. She does not know if he is in hiding, or if he has been detained or killed.
Not long after he disappeared, she says masked men - some dressed in military clothes - visited and took a number of Abu Obeid's possessions, including his laptop and other devices.

The wishes of Abu Obeid's wife now chillingly mirror those of Tice's mother and family. On opposite sides of a disappearance that began more than a decade ago, both families are searching for the same thing: a loved one who vanished, and an answer to where he went.

MANILA, Philippines – Scam compounds linked to Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGOs) have become a major organized crime problem in the country, with human trafficking, online scams, and other criminal activities converging in the same operations.

Former Presidential Anti-Organized Crime Commission (PAOCC) officials Winnie Quidato and Winston Casio draw on their experience dismantling scam compounds in their new book, The Rogue Compound: POGOs, Human Trafficking, and the Fight to Reclaim the Philippines.

On Friday, September 18, Rappler editor-at-large Marites Vitug speaks to Quidato and Casio about how scam compounds took root in the Philippines, the challenges law enforcement faced in going after them, and what it takes to dismantle these criminal networks.

Quidato is a retired police officer with decades of experience in intelligence work. He spent three years working to dismantle scam compounds as PAOCC deputy executive director. Casio, meanwhile, is a crime analyst and educator who served as PAOCC spokesperson.
With the Anti-POGO Act now in place, do POGOs still operate underground?
Catch the interview on Thursday at 6 pm! – Rappler.com

articles.title: Can impeachment court decisions be appealed to SC?
articles.summary: Former associate justice Azcuna says the Supreme Court may reverse the Senate's ruling on the conviction threshold, but retired chief justice Panganiban says the High Court should not intervene

blocks.text: Former Chief Justices Artemio Panganiban and Reynato Puno, and retired Associate Justice Adolf Azcuna, appearing as amici curiae, advised the impeachment court on the conviction threshold debate whether the vote threshold should be based on the full membership of 24 senators or only those able to participate, on September 16, 2026.
Senate Social Media Unit
Former associate justice Azcuna says the Supreme Court may reverse the Senate's ruling on the conviction threshold, but retired chief justice Panganiban says the High Court should not intervene

items: The impeachment court sought advice from former justices regarding the conviction threshold and the potential for Supreme Court intervention in the Senate's decisions.

Retired justices indicated that while the Senate has the authority to decide impeachment cases, the Supreme Court can review decisions if there is grave abuse of discretion or violation of due process.

The ongoing debate about the two-thirds vote requirement for conviction may lead to judicial challenges, especially if the threshold is altered, with Vice President Duterte's legal team likely to pursue judicial relief.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

When the impeachment court invited former magistrates to seek their advice, not only did senators get the legal luminaries’ take on the conviction threshold debate, but also asked them on whether the path the Senate takes can be appealed before the Supreme Court.

Nothing stops Vice President Sara Duterte — and also her critics — from pursuing a path to judicial relief should the impeachment court’s decisions favor their foes, but the former SC justices’ answers on Wednesday, September 16, offered insights on how contentious this issue can be.

Retired associate justice Adolfo Azcuna’s answer was straightforward: only the SC has the final say on interpretation of constitutional boundaries. He believes the High Court can step in and reverse a Senate impeachment court ruling, should it decide to adjust the minimum number needed to convict the Vice President.

“I think there may be grounds for intervention by the Supreme Court if someone who remains a senator, despite not participating in the trial for one reason or another, is excluded from the denominator when determining the required vote,” Azcuna told the impeachment court.

The issue at hand concerns the interpretation of Article 11, Section 3(6) of the Constitution, which states: “No person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the members of the Senate.”

Should “all” in that constitutional provision refer to 24 — the total composition of the Senate — when there are at least four absentee senators? Senators Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada are in jail due to plunder charges; Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is in hiding in connection with his International Criminal Court drug war case; and Senator Loren Legarda has been on medical leave.

Retired SC chief justices Artemio Panganiban and Reynato Puno said that as a general rule, the Senate exercises judicial power as the sole body with the power to try and decide impeachment cases. As the proceedings are sui generis (a class of its own), its decisions settle what are largely political questions.
However, there are exceptions. They said judicial review can be made by the High Court when the impeachment court commits grave abuse of discretion or violates a party’s right to due process.

“If the Senate commits grave abuse of discretion, then the Supreme Court will have to take action. Not because the Supreme Court is higher than the Senate, but because it is just exercising a power lodged in it by the Constitution,” Panganiban said.

blocks.caption: Can impeachment court decisions be appealed to SC?

blocks.text: Some senator-judges, in their interjections, appeared to anticipate arguments of grave abuse of discretion that could be raised before the SC in the future.
Senator Kiko Pangilinan asked the former justices whether voting to change the basis for the two-thirds threshold would violate Duterte’s right to due process.
“Commendably, you are doing this meeting so that you cannot be accused of grave abuse of discretion if it ever comes down to that,” Panganiban said. “I think you have been very prudent.”
Panganiban, responding to another question by Senator Ping Lacson, said he believed that the SC should not interfere on the conviction threshold issue.

“Were you capricious? Were you whimsical? Were you arbitrary in making your decision? If you are debating about it, and in fact, you called the sweethearts of the Supreme Court to help you with this short of telling you what the decision should be… Supreme Court should not intervene,” Panganiban said.

The amici curiae was conducted after Senator Erwin Tulfo pushed to revisit presiding officer Senator Chiz Escudero’s initial decision on the conviction threshold. At the start of the trial in July, he kept the number at 16 votes, citing a 2000 SC ruling that upheld the constitutionality of the Senate’s ratification of the Visiting Forces Agreement. Bayan v Zamora kept the two-thirds threshold requirement in treaty ratifications at 16 votes despite the Senate lacking one member.
On Wednesday, Escudero said he issued his ruling in July in hopes that someone would raise the issue before the SC for a final determination early on.

He explained that he wanted to prevent a scenario where the impeachment court’s eventual decision on whether to convict or acquit the Vice President will be undermined by an unresolved debate on the conviction threshold.

Wednesday’s amici curiae makes it appear that prosecutors may not necessarily need 16 votes to win the case. Only Azcuna stuck with the 16-vote-threshold view, while Panganiban, Puno, and former chief justice Hilario Davide Jr., through a written position, shied away from a literal interpretation of the 1987 Constitution.

If Escudero — or the impeachment court — is swayed into lowering the threshold, expect the Vice President to knock on the SC’s doors. Her legal team has a penchant for seeking judicial relief every step of the way in the impeachment process, even when it was still in the early stages in the House of Representatives.

In fact, when when Escudero announced the amici curiae on September 8, the Duterte camp made sure to manifest that the defense team’s participation would be made ad cautelam, or strictly out of abundant caution. The court is slated to make a decision after the oral arguments on September 23.
“Such decision is without prejudice to any legal remedies that any of the parties may take,” defense lawyer Michael Poa manifested on September 8. – Rappler.com

articles.summary: COTABATO CITY – The Philippine National Police (PNP) commended and rewarded with cash assistance a police officer who was wounded while performing poll duties during the historic Bangsamoro elections…

blocks.text: COTABATO CITY – The Philippine National Police (PNP) commended and rewarded with cash assistance a police officer who was wounded while performing poll duties during the historic Bangsamoro elections last Monday.
Lt. Gen. Wilson Joseph Lopez, PNP deputy chief for operations, visited Patrolman Justeen Reo Ga at the Notre Dame Hospital here on Tuesday and assured him of government financial support.

Ga, who is assigned at the Dinagat Islands Police Provincial Office, was among four people injured in the attack by armed men inside the Cotabato City Central Pilot Elementary School during the early hours of the Bangsamoro parliamentary elections. There was one fatality.

“The incident underscored the risks faced by police personnel on the front lines of election security as they carry out their duty to protect voters, election workers, and the integrity of the electoral process,” Lopez said.
He handed over financial support to the wounded police officer and assured that his welfare, morale, and proper medical care will remain a priority./coa

articles.title: Carpio will seek SC help if Congress passes House's anti-political dynasty bill
articles.summary: Retired Supreme Court (SC) Associate Justice Antonio Carpio on Thursday said they will seek recourse from the High Court should Congress pass the controversial anti-political dynasty bill principally…

blocks.text: Published September 17, 2026 12:07pm

Retired Supreme Court (SC) Associate Justice Antonio Carpio on Thursday said they will seek recourse from the High Court should Congress pass the controversial anti-political dynasty bill principally authored by Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III and House Majority Leader Ferdinand Alexander “Sandro” Marcos.

Carpio said the bill, which bans relatives up to the second degree of consanguinity or affinity from running for or occupying a post in the same constituency or jurisdiction, only legitimizes political dynasties.

“Kapag pinasa nila itong Speaker (Dy)-Sandro Marcos’ bill na inapprove na ng House, di ba? Hindi kami sang-ayon diyan sa bill na ‘yan, we will go to the SC and say, hindi ito anti-political dynasty law,” he said in an interview on Super Radyo dzBB.

(If they pass this Speaker (Dy)-Sandro Marcos’ bill that was already approved by the House, right? We do not agree with that bill; we will go to the SC and say, this is not an anti-political dynasty law.)
“This is a political dynasty legitimization and entrenchment law,” he added.
The SC has directed Congress to enact an anti-political dynasty law at the earliest opportunity, saying its failure to do so for 39 years constitutes grave abuse of discretion.
The SC, however, is leaving it to Congress to define what constitutes a political dynasty and determine the scope of the prohibition.

In June, the House of Representatives passed on third and final reading an anti-political dynasty bill that would ban relatives up to the second degree of consanguinity or affinity from running for or occupying a post in the same constituency or jurisdiction.
For his part, Marcos said that the bill is not yet set in stone as revisions can still be made during the deliberations of the bicameral conference committee
According to Carpio, they will mount a people’s initiative to enact a “genuine anti-political dynasty law.”
“We do not agree with the Marcos bill passed by the House,” he said. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: DOF seeks to triple sugary drinks tax
articles.summary: The Department of Finance said higher taxes on sugary drinks is not only a revenue collection policy, but also a health measure.

blocks.text: September 17, 2026 | 12:07pm
Close-up of colorful beverage cans arranged closely together.
Breakingpic via Pexels
MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Finance (DOF) is pushing to raise taxes on sugary drinks to at least three times their current rate to discourage consumption.

The finance department said Thursday, September 17, that its goal in imposing higher taxes on sweetened drinks is not only to generate revenue, but also to address and curb lifestyle diseases like diabetes, obesity and kidney issues among Filipinos.

“Gusto natin bawasan o i-discourage ang pagkonsumo ng mga sweetened beverages kasi nakita natin, at sabi din ng mga eksperto din sa health sector, na talagang nagdudulot ito ng mga sakit,” DOF Assistance Secretary for Revenue Operations Group Euvimil Nina Asuncion told dzMM in an interview.
(We want to reduce or discourage the consumption of sweetened beverages because we saw, and even the experts in the health sector said, that this causes diseases.)

Based on the Philippine Statistics Authority’s (PSA) report released June 30, diabetes ranked fifth among the leading causes of death in the Philippines in 2026, with 2,795 recorded deaths as of February.
Meanwhile, the National Nutrition Council said on September 10 that 43% of Filipino adults are obese.
The government currently imposes a P6 to P12 per liter excise tax on pre-packed sweetened drinks under Republic Act No. 10963, or the Philippine TRAIN Law.
The DOF, however, proposed to raise these taxes from P6 to P20 per liter for non-caloric and caloric beverages, and from P12 to P40 for drinks using fructose corn syrup.

Should the finance department’s proposal be approved, retail prices of carbonated soft drinks, pre-packed teas and other ready-to-drink juices that are widely available in the market could also increase.
But, unlike previous measures, the DOF is also currently proposing that these excise taxes on sugary drinks be adjusted by around 5% every year.
“Gusto talaga natin na imbes na magkonsumo sila ng softdrinks…iinom sila ng healthier na alternative,” Asuncion said.
(We want them to consume healthier alternatives instead of consuming softdrinks.)
The collected taxes from these products are intended to support Universal Health Care, which enrolls all Filipinos into the country’s national health insurance, according to Asuncion.

articles.title: ‘Like a Disney movie’: Three wild dog brothers make Africa’s longest journey
articles.summary:
As three siblings came of age and had to leave their pack, scientists tracked the dogs’ perilous 2,500-mile odyssey to find their own territory

It sounds like a Disney movie: three wild…
articles.byline: Patrick Greenfield. Photographs by Scott Creel

blocks.text: It sounds like a Disney movie: three wild dogs, all brothers, on an epic journey to find a home of their own after their family tells them to leave. They dodge cars and hunters in search of a new life, navigating bushmeat snares and the hostility of a human-dominated landscape until they find a new haven on the African savannah.

But this is exactly what happened in Zambia last year, when three endangered African wild dogs made the longest-ever recorded single journey of any mammal from the continent. The brothers travelled more than 2,500 miles (4,100km) over eight months in their “dispersal” – when a young dog comes of age and must establish new territory to find a mate and start a family of their own.

blocks.caption: Two months after they set out, the brothers and sisters met again, spending a day together before separating.  Photograph: MSU

blocks.text: From point to point, starting in Kafue national park in western Zambia to their final destination in the Luangwa valley in the east of the country, the brothers covered 340 miles (546km), which is also a record.

The epic single journey is almost equivalent to travelling the length of Chile by foot and farther than the famous wildebeest and zebra migration across the Serengeti in east Africa. The previous record was 2,418 miles, also made by African wild dogs, which moved between Loliondo, in northern Tanzania’s Ngorongoro district, and Tsavo West national park in southern Kenya in 2012.

Dr Matt Becker, chief executive of the Zambian Carnivore Programme (ZCP), whose scientists were monitoring the wild dogs and have published their findings in the journal Ecology, says: “These extraordinary journeys show that natural connections between Africa’s wildlife strongholds still exist. But they also reveal how difficult and dangerous those journeys have become.

“Rather than relying solely on fenced protected areas, these findings reinforce the value of investing in connected landscapes. The dogs are showing us that connectivity still works; now we need to do more to protect and strengthen it.”

The researchers tracked 19 separate groups of wild dogs to monitor their dispersals, including a group of sisters to the three brothers who were far less successful at finding a new range. Two of the sisters died, probably caught in snares, but not before they had a touching final encounter with their siblings.

Two months into their journey, the group of brothers and sisters came across each other deep in Zambia’s copper-belt mining region, spending the day together before going their separate ways again. Related dogs do not form new family packs, and typically have to travel long distances through the landscape to find prospective mates.

Only 6,600 or so adults remain of 39 distinct populations of African wild dogs, and the species is classified as endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list. Habitat loss, declining numbers of natural prey, bushmeat hunters’ snares and human conflict are among the biggest threats to their survival.

But researchers say the three brothers’ epic journey shows the wild dogs can still survive in a human-dominated landscape despite the enormous challenges they face. Alongside African savannah elephants, whose ancient migration routes are increasingly being blocked by human development, African wild dogs need to be able to make long journeys to find new homes.

“These long-term studies provide key evidence that connectivity between large landscapes is still there,” says Dr Nyambe Nyambe, director of the Kavango-Zambezi transfrontier area secretariat, a key conservation region that spans five countries, including Zambia, where governments are trying to keep space for wildlife to move through the landscape.

blocks.caption: African wild dogs have been endangered for decades, with only 6,600 or so adults remaining of 39 populations across the continent.  Photograph: MSU

blocks.text: “If we conserve and continue to improve these connections – spanning the range of national parks, community areas, nations and regions – a lot of species like wild dogs can make the rest happen,” Nyambe says.
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

articles.title: English Heritage trains new generation of scythers to maintain meadows and craft
articles.summary:
Initiative aims to keep alive age-old skill, and at Muchelney Abbey in Somerset improve habitat for rare shrill carder bee

It sounds like something out of a Thomas Hardy novel: a merry band…

blocks.text: It sounds like something out of a Thomas Hardy novel: a merry band of men and women roaming the West Country cutting meadows by hand in exchange for hunks of bread and cheese.
But the conservation charity English Heritage is recruiting a team of volunteer scythers to maintain 21st-century meadowland in the old-fashioned way.

The first scythers have been trained and will use their new skills in the meadows around an abbey in Somerset, where it is hoped that as well as helping to keep the age-old practice alive, they will protect a rare type of bumblebee.

blocks.caption: James Adams scything at Muchelney Abbey, which will be the focus of the first English Heritage scything project. Photograph: Andre Pattenden/English Heritage/PA

blocks.text: Ginny Slade, who has completed the training, said she found there was something therapeutic about scything.

“You need a level of physical fitness but it’s also about enthusiasm and the passion to learn heritage skills,” she said. “It’s a repetitive movement. You find your rhythm and zone into it. You can really connect with the meadow, the landscape.”
The first volunteers have also found that using the scythe is something of a sensual treat – the sound of the blade cutting, the scent of the meadow.

Slade said: “Scything is a wonderful example of how traditional skills can still have a role in addressing modern challenges. We hope to help create the diverse, flower-rich habitats that pollinators need while also preserving knowledge and skills that have shaped our landscapes.”

Slade, a volunteer and community engagement manager with English Heritage, is one of the first to be trained by professionals at the Exmoor National Park Authority in the art of using and maintaining a scythe. “You want a really good scythe,” said Slade. “If you look after them, they can last generations.”
English Heritage rewards volunteers with bread and cheese (it also thought about providing West Country cider but thought this was not a good idea on health and safety grounds).

The first group of scythers will help care for the meadow at Muchelney Abbey, in Somerset, which was once a wealthy and important monastery with features including a thatched two-storey monks’ lavatory, which is unique in Britain.

They will work on a three-year project with the Bumblebee Conservation Trust to improve habitat for the shrill carder bee, a species that has declined significantly because of the loss of flower-rich grasslands.

blocks.caption: A shrill carder bee. Photograph: Kevin Rushby/The Guardian

blocks.text: As part of the project, English Heritage volunteers have been trained by the bumblebee trust to carry out wildlife surveys.

Rather than simply recording numbers, volunteers will monitor the relationship between bees and the meadow ecosystem, including which flowers are in bloom, which plants they are using, how far bees travel from their nests and how the habitat changes over time.

Hardy wrote about scything in prose and poetry: in Far From the Madding Crowd, Bathsheba Everdene watches haymaking, and the farm hand Mark Clark is described as “humming a tune to the strokes of his scythe”.
In his poem Four in the Morning, Hardy wrote about the “to-and-fro/Wheezed whettings of a scythe apace”.
The meadow at Muchelney is one of 100 that English Heritage pledged to create and enhance to mark the coronation of King Charles in 2023.

Slade said Muchelney was the pilot site but the idea was for the volunteers to travel to other English Heritage sites to use their skills. “We’re really at the beginning of this journey, but we’re very excited about it.”

articles.title: Turkey detains dozens in crackdown on LGBTQ+ activists and journalists
articles.summary:
Protesters teargassed as minister claims widespread raids and arrests under obscenity laws were to ‘protect families’

Turkish authorities have used accusations of obscenity to justify a…

blocks.text: Turkish authorities have used accusations of obscenity to justify a wave of raids and arrests targeting the LGBTQ+ community, which has grown to include journalists as well as more than 150 arrested during protests against the raids.

Starting in the early hours of Sunday, Turkish police carried out simultaneous raids on the offices of LGBTQ+ rights organisations and HIV-advocacy groups in the cities of Istanbul, the capital, Ankara, and the coastal city of İzmir, as well as the cities of Aydın and Mersin.
“This is the widest crackdown on LGBTQ+ people in recent years,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb, of Human Rights Watch.

Video released by the Turkish interior ministry showed police rummaging through filing cabinets, grabbing rainbow flags and leading people away in handcuffs, as well as raiding nightclubs and the homes of activists.
Prosecutors in Istanbul said officials seized digital equipment, drugs and a firearm, as well as arresting dozens of people in the raids.

Rights groups tracking the arrests believe that 62 people have been held on remand, but more than 100 were detained. Sinclair-Webb, who accused authorities of attempting to smear and criminalise LGBTQ+ advocacy, said: “We believe this includes others not associated with LGBTQ+ groups [detained] for drug and prostitution offences.”

While homosexuality is not illegal in Turkey, prosecutors in Ankara have accused LGBTQ+ rights groups of violating laws prohibiting “obscenity”, and those governing NGOs, although formal charges remain opaque.

Turkey’s justice minister, Akın Gürlek, said the raids and arrests across the country were part of an operation entitled “My Family is Safe” and claimed the sweep was intended to “protect our children, the institution of the family and the social order”.
As a result, Gürlek said, authorities targeted venues they claimed were associated with prostitution, distribution of obscene material “and activities exposing children to such content”.

blocks.caption: Protesters in İzmir are treated after riot police used teargas during a demonstration against the detention of 16 people in government raids on LGBTQ+ groups.  Photograph: Ali Dinç/Reuters

blocks.text: A Turkish press freedom group, the Media and Law Studies Association, said this included seven members of the executive board of Kaos GL, one of Turkey’s oldest LGBTQ+ advocacy groups that also operates a news site.

Tuğba Tekerek, a journalist, was arrested at her home in Istanbul and taken to Ankara for questioning by prosecutors, after publishing a piece with Kaos GL on the LGBTQ+ community in the neighbouring country of Georgia.

As the initial raids sparked protests, the wave of arrests grew this week. Turkish authorities teargassed hundreds of protesters in İzmir, and detained at least 150 demonstrators in Istanbul on Tuesday as well as dozens more in Ankara.

The French news agency AFP reported that several of the arrests outside a courthouse in Istanbul took place after demonstrators unfurled a banner that read “Being LGBTQ+ is not a crime” and chanted “Long live the struggle for freedom.”
A draft amendment to Turkey’s penal code that proposed prosecuting all LGBTQ+ people in Turkey for promoting behaviour “contrary to biological sex and general morality” was withdrawn last year.

Instead, the Turkish authorities have increasingly targeted LGBTQ+ individuals and groups using broad “obscenity” charges. Eleven leaders of the Genç LGBTI+ [Youth LGBTI+] organisation went on trial last month, accused of violating constitutional provisions on “family values” and publishing images showing same-sex couples kissing, charges that carry up to three years’ imprisonment.

The justice minister linked the launch of the “My Family is Safe” campaign to a directive launched by the president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, declaring what he called “a decade of the family and population” and aiming to boost birthrates.

“Our family ties are weakening, the average age of marriage is rising, divorce rates are increasing and as a result, our fertility rate is declining. To be honest, the statistics are alarming for all of us,” Gürlek said.

But rights groups have questioned how arresting LGBTQ+ activists and demonstrators protects Turkish families. Sinclair-Webb said: “Obviously, protecting children and the family is important – no one is debating that – but in a country with a large and concerning record of domestic violence, many cases of child abuse and murders of women, the protection of the family cannot be focused on LGBT people.”
