articles.title: Chancellor Merz seeks CDU support as AfD encroaches
articles.summary: Following the CDU's crushing defeat in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, many are expressing doubts about the party's leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz. But the CDU doesn't appear to have a viable…

image.caption: Chancellor Friedrich Merz has seen his support wane in recent monthsImage: dts-Agentur/picture alliance

blocks.text: Earlier this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was in Rovaniemi in northern Finland — nearly 1,800 kilometers (about 1,100 miles) north of Berlin — but even that wasn't far enough to escape the unrest brewing in the German capital. Representatives from various countries had gathered there for the European Arctic Summit to discuss natural resources, geopolitics, security and climate change.
When asked by journalists about the mood in Berlin, the chancellor said he could understand the heated debate in Germany surrounding him but that the future of Europe was far more urgent.

"That's why I'm trying to convince my friends, my political party, and my parliamentary caucus that this is important — much more important than some of the domestic political debates we're having," he said.

Merz was referring to the discussions and rumors circulating about whether he is still the right person for the job — not even a year and a half after he took office as German chancellor back in May 2025. That's because public support for the federal government has hit a record low, and the chancellor's party, the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), recently suffered a crushing defeat in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt.
Why is Merz so unpopular?

Another heavy defeat looks likely in the state election coming up in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. In the lead-up to voting on September 20, the chancellor's party is polling at a dramatically low 7%. Failure to clear the 5% hurdle to enter the state parliament even seems possible. Whatever happens, the CDU is likely to record its worst-ever results in a state election.

The election earlier this month in Saxony-Anhalt was won by the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, the domestic intelligence agency, in this central German state.

Before taking office, Merz promised he would cut support for the AfD "in half." Instead, support for Merz's own party has dropped by half, and political circles in Berlin are asking: Is this Merz's fault? Is it perhaps due to his often abrasive communication style, or his failure to clearly explain important reforms — such as the one regarding the state pension system?
German Chancellor Merz reels as far-right AfD makes gains

Members of the government are speaking openly about the lack of trust in the Merz cabinet. Education Minister Karin Prien (also of the CDU), for example, said on the public broadcaster ARD: "I believe that many people feel that the chancellor — and we in the CDU/CSU as well — lack the necessary empathy. And that has to change."

One frequently heard view is that Merz often comes across as lacking restraint. The planned pension reform, for example, would mean difficult cuts for many, but Merz often seems impatient when discussing it, commentators say. Back in July, the chancellor complained publicly that many citizens' attitudes about a "four-day workweek and work-life balance" could jeopardize the country's prosperity. Trade union representatives were outraged that the chancellor had accused Germans of being "lazy."
When the microphones and cameras are off, governing officials speak even more bluntly. The center-left Social Democrats (SPD), the CDU's junior coalition partner, are also sounding the alarm.

"You really get the impression that nerves are a bit frayed in the CDU right now," said SPD Parliamentary Secretary Dirk Wiese on the Welt TV channel. "I can only appeal once again to our coalition partner to really get back on track and work with us to do things better."

blocks.caption: Henrik Wüst (center) is often named as a possible successor to Friedrich Merz Image: Revierfoto/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Two chancellor candidates: Söder and Wüst
But the problem remains that even if the CDU and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), agree that Merz must step down as chancellor, there is no clear successor.
SU leader Markus Söder, the Bavarian state premier, has been named as a possible candidate. However, he often and readily provokes the CDU and therefore lacks broad support within the party.

Another candidate would be Hendrik Wüst, the CDU state premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populous state. Although he has quite capably led a coalition with the environmentalist Green Party for over four years, he has so far shown little inclination to move to Berlin. And most importantly, Wüst plans to run for reelection next April in North Rhine-Westphalia.

Provided there was enough support for a change of leadership in the governing coalition, there would be no major procedural challenges. Following the resignation of the chancellor, a successor is then appointed by parliamentary majority in the Bundestag.

However, if the sitting chancellor doesn't voluntarily step down, a "constructive vote of no confidence" is required. In this case, Wüst or Söder would have to openly challenge Merz — a scenario that no one can imagine at the moment.

Perhaps for this reason, too, all eight CDU state premiers declared in a joint statement on Wednesday that they still stood behind Merz. The statement reads: "People can trust that we will address their problems. As state premiers, we want to — and will — contribute to this effort together with the chancellor."

Germany needs "stability more than ever," the premiers said on Wednesday, calling for unity within the CDU and arguing that the way to rebuild voters' trust was through "listening and political action, not personnel debates."

blocks.caption: Markus Söder (left) has long been rumored to have ambitions for the German chancellorshipImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The statement was signed by all eight premiers: Daniel Günther of Schleswig-Holstein, Boris Rhein of Hesse, Sven Schulze of Saxony-Anhalt, Kai Wegner of Berlin, Michael Kretschmer of Saxony, Gordon Schnieder of Rhineland-Palatinate, Mario Voigt of Thuringia and Wüst of North Rhine-Westphalia.
Pivotal state elections coming up
So while there isn't really a clear alternative to Merz, the chancellor also isn't someone who is likely to simply step down.

If rumors circulating in political circles in Berlin are to be believed, Merz wants to convene the executive committee of the CDU in Berlin as early as this coming Sunday evening, once the results of the state election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania are in. His plan is to stand in front of this group of 22 leading conservative politicians and pose the question of whether his party is still willing to put its trust in him.

Merz's schedule for the coming week illustrates just how seriously he views the situation. The chancellor has canceled his trip to the United Nations General Assembly, an engagement that had been planned well in advance and was treated as a fixed appointment. "Contrary to the original plans, he will not travel to New York, as he is needed in Berlin," government sources have confirmed.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Can Canada and the EU build a deeper partnership?
articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Carney is known for standing up to US President Donald Trump. Now he wants to forge a "unique alliance" with Europe. But what could such a partnership look like?

image.caption: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney (center) met with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen (left) and European Council President Antonio Costa (right) in Brussels in 2025Image: Sean Kilpatrick/empics/picture alliance

blocks.text: Before taking off for Europe, CanadianPrime Minister Mark Carney had set the tone for his visit, saying he was seeking to build a "unique alliance" with the EU. The Wall Street Journal similarly reported that Canada was considering becoming an "associate member" of the EU, while not aiming for full membership.
In her State of the European Union address on Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen indicated that she was indeed open to such an expanded partnership.

"We believe that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest, but to all of us," she said, addressing European lawmakers and Carney in Strasbourg, France. "That democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work."

Von der Leyen said a EU-Canada partnership would cover a broad range of areas including advanced manufacturing, technology, defense production, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, cybersecurity and economic security.
Carney is expected to outline his vision for future relations between the EU and Canada during a speech at the European Parliament on Thursday.
What degree of collaboration could be possible between the EU and Canada?

EU member states are closely integrated economically, sharing a common market, trade and customs policy. When it comes to establishing ties with non-EU countries, a list of different options present themselves. They range from free trade agreements that scrap tariffs and trade barriers, to association agreements which may include political elements, to far-reaching economic arrangements such as participation in the common European market, as is the case for Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway.

blocks.caption: At the World Economic Forum in January, Mark Carney said there had been a "rupture in the world order" Image: Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The EU has already negotiated association agreements with Turkey, Israel and Ukraine. These have different objectives and may or may not mark a preliminary step toward full membership.

Patrick Leblond, an expert on international economic relations at the University of Ottawa, urges a little more caution around the term "association agreement." He considers it unlikely that Canada would adopt European laws or join the EU single market or customs union, which would mean imposing common external tariffs.
Leblond says Carney is likely more interested in forming a kind of alliance that deepens cooperation on issues of economic security and defense.
Closer defense cooperation?
"We have, in a way, taken the US [security] umbrella for granted on both sides. We have underinvested in our militaries," Leblond told DW.
He added that the focus was now on joining forces, for example in the production of military equipment and the development of new technologies.

Security analyst Anand Sundar of the European Council on Foreign Relations also sees great potential for European-Canadian cooperation when it comes to defense. Canada spends about 70% of its defense budget on US-made equipment, according to Sundar. Carney wants to change that, the analyst said, as it would pay off for Canadians to be part of European defense projects to get "more bang for their buck."

Canada has joined the EU's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program. It provides EU member states with up to €150 billion ($173 billion, CA$ 241 billion) in loans for the joint procurement of military equipment. To qualify for funding, no more than 35% of the cost of the components can come from countries outside the EU, the European Economic Area (EEA) or Ukraine. Yet because Canada joined the SAFE program by paying a fee, more lenient procurement rules apply to its companies.

Nevertheless, Canadian companies still face significant hurdles for producing and purchasing weapons in partnership with European firms, Sundar told DW. The big question is how far the EU is willing to relax its own rules, the expert says, which could also have implications for non-EU countries, such as the United Kingdom or Norway.
'Underrated defense power'
"But the biggest draw for the European Union is really the fact that that Canada is an underrated defense power," Sundar told DW.
Canada, the expert added, spends more on defense than the 14 smallest EU member states combined.

The North American country invests 2% of its gross domestic product (GDP) on defense, Sundar said, with an increase expected in the coming years. Canada, like other NATO countries, has committed to spending a total of 5% of its GDP on defense by 2035, of which 3.5% will go towards military equipment and the remaining 1.5% towards other defense-related areas.
Protecting critical infrastructure

The EU and Canada also intend to discuss potential cooperation in the field of critical infrastructure expansion, such as the joint operation of space satellites or maintenance of fiber-optic cables in the North Atlantic, Leblond told DW. The goal here, too, is to become less dependent on the US and its companies. Moreover, Canada has oil and gas reserves that could meet some of the bloc's energy demands.

Trade relations between both have already been codified through the EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which entered into force on a provisional basis in September 2017. The agreement eliminates nearly all tariffs between the EU and Canada, while also ensuring mutual market access for industrial goods, agricultural products and services. It even enables European companies to participate in public tenders in Canada.

Economic analyst Leblond, however, believes that CETA's potential has not yet been fully realized. He says many Canadian companies still tend to focus on the US and less on Europe. He believes it is the government's responsibility to provide more information about CETA and the opportunities it offers, saying the level of exchange envisaged in this format could also be intensified.
Why is Carney seeking closer ties with Europe?
In January, Carney delivered a speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos in which he warned of a "rupture in the world order," calling on the middle powers to act together.
"If we're not at the table, we're on the menu," he said.
Indeed, in recent weeks, the US-Canda trade war has continued escalating.

Even though it is clear that Canada cannot sever ties with the US, there is a growing belief inside Canada that the country needs additional allies, Leblond told DW. And the Europeans are considered trustworthy, he added.
Ultimately, the Canadians would want to see such an alliance, whatever form it may take, translate into concrete initiatives and projects through which Europeans and Canadians can help one another.
This article was translated from German

articles.title: Photos show widespread damage at US sites from Iranian attacks
articles.summary: A wrecked air force plane and destroyed buildings are among the images obtained by the BBC's partner CBS News.
articles.byline: Kayla Epstein and Bernd Debusmann Jr

blocks.text: Images showing widespread damage to multiple US sites in the Middle East from Iranian strikes have been obtained by the BBC's US partner CBS.
The photos, provided by active military personnel, show a severed radar jet, flattened trailers and severely damaged buildings.
The undated photos were taken at US bases and sites in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait.
One member of the military, who was not named by CBS, said: "This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public.
"We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face."
The White House referred the BBC to US Central Command. Centcom did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The photos, which have not been independently verified by the BBC, were published the day after a report from the Pentagon's watchdog confirmed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in the Middle East have been damaged and destroyed by Iran.
One of the photos showed a destroyed Boeing E-3 Sentry at Prince Sultan Air Force Base in Saudi Arabia that has been ripped in half, its tail section crumpled into a tangled mess of metal.

The images were published on the heels of a report from the Pentagon's watchdog, which found Iranian strikes had "damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict".
It also noted that equipment losses have totalled $3.7bn (£2.8bn). Overall, the US spent $33.4bn (£24.7bn) on the war up to 29 June, the report said.
In the months after the war began, "dozens of US aircraft were destroyed or damaged", the report continues.
The document lists several of the aircraft damaged, including five refuelling aircraft which were "damaged or destroyed on the ground in Saudi Arabia by Iranian munitions".
A separate report , externalfrom the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) notes that the E-3 aircraft is no longer in production and would have to be replaced with a more modern equivalent, the E-7.

The CBO noted that the E-3 aircraft alone costs $500m (£371m), and the estimated total cost of equipment lost in battle - including planes, drones and a terminal high altitude area defence system - amounts to $1.9b (£1.4b).

CBO said that its review was subject to "uncertainty" because the defence department did not respond to its requests for information, requiring the agency to rely on government databases and public reports.
Additionally, the extent of repairs and rebuilding that the US military plans to do remains unclear, according to the report.
Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country.
Since the war began Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel.

On Tuesday night, the US House of Representatives voted for the third time to end the war in Iran, approving a measure that would force President Donald Trump to end US military action without congressional approval.
The vote passed with the help of several Republicans, in what could be the final House vote on the matter ahead of the US midterm elections in November.
It faces an uncertain path to passage - the US Senate has not indicated if it will take up the matter.
The same day, outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie announced an attempt to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth as new details emerged about the Iran war's price tag for the US.
The Trump administration backed Hegseth, with US attorney general Todd Blanche telling reporters he was "doing a phenomenal job".

articles.title: Pia Cayetano: 'I fear for my right to speak'
articles.summary: Senator Pia Cayetano on Wednesday said she was feeling fear and pressure as more members of the minority bloc face cases amid the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published September 17, 2026 12:00am
Senator Pia Cayetano on Wednesday said she was feeling fear and pressure as more members of the minority bloc face cases amid the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

During a session where senator-judges heard insights from four retired Supreme justices on the voting threshold for conviction, Cayetano said she had observed that several senators had been unable to attend the hearings.

Currently, Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained over separate plunder charges, while Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is in hiding amid an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in connection with the Duterte administration’s war on drugs.
Senator Loren Legarda has not attended the trial for several weeks as she remains abroad on extended medical leave.

“I went to Singapore to support a national team, and then I have to hear the NBI director making statements that make it appear that I’m a common fugitive, na na-monitor niya kung nasaan ako at meron siyang information kung anong araw ako babalik. Am I a fugitive? Bakit may ganito? (That he monitored where I was and had information on when I would return. Am I a fugitive? Why is it like this?)” Cayetano said.

“I will tell you all now, am I pressured? I am. I am. I fear for my liberty. Even in the Senate, we have a colleague, na walang katapusang tantanan kami (Even in the Senate, we have a colleague who just won’t stop going after us.). I fear for my right to speak,” she added.

“So, what will happen now? Do I excuse myself? Pero kung hindi gagalawin 'yang number na iyan eh di nakakapagsalita tayo rito nang maayos (But if that number is not changed, then we can speak freely here),” she said, apparently referring to Presiding Officer Francis Escudero’s ruling that under the 1987 Constitution conviction requires at least 16 affirmative votes, or two-thirds of all members of the Senate.
Senator Pia Cayetano and her brother, Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano, traveled to Singapore on September 9 and returned to the Philippines on September 12.
According to the Bureau of Immigration, there was no hold departure order or derogatory record that would have prevented the Cayetanos from traveling abroad. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: DepEd taps 170 leaders to boost SHS graduates’ employability
articles.summary: The Department of Education has tapped the assistance of more than 170 leaders across government, industry and strategic economic sectors in implementing the work immersion program under the…

blocks.text: September 17, 2026 | 12:00am
Education Secretary Sonny Angara.
DepEd Facebook page

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Education (DepEd) has tapped the assistance of more than 170 leaders across government, industry and strategic economic sectors in implementing the work immersion program under the Strengthened Senior High School (SHS) curriculum to improve the employability of graduates.
Education Secretary Sonny Angara said closing the gap between schools and industry requires urgent, ground-level execution.

The DepEd is streamlining the senior high school framework from four tracks to two: Academic and Technical-Professional (TechPro), giving learners greater subject flexibility while embedding intensive, industry-guided work immersion options.
For TechPro learners, the enhanced work immersion program will feature structured joint training plans, hands-on mentoring and industry assessments tied directly to national skills certifications.

Industry leaders underscored the need to embed strict workplace safety standards, essential soft skills and ethical values into early career training to help learners succeed in high-demand environments.
Partner associations expressed strong support for structured immersion models, with initial industry commitments already pledging around 31,000 work immersion slots.
This represents more than 60 percent of DepEd’s 50,000-slot target across over 1,100 distinct job roles.

“We are refining our curriculum and expanding our Enhanced Work Immersion Program because our learners deserve real pathways to quality jobs, entrepreneurship and higher learning. We cannot build a future-ready economy with yesterday’s skills framework,” Angara said.

articles.title: DBM: 94.1% of 2026 budget released
articles.summary: The Marcos administration has released roughly 94.1 percent of the P6.793-trillion national budget as of end-August, a slightly slower pace than the previous year’s, the Department of Budget…

blocks.text: September 17, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Marcos administration has released roughly 94.1 percent of the P6.793-trillion national budget as of end-August, a slightly slower pace than the previous year’s, the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) said.
Data from the Status of Allotment Releases report showed that the DBM released P6.39 trillion in the first eight months of the year, representing 94.1 percent of the total allocation.
This leaves about P401.38 billion still to be released in the remaining four months.
The releases are behind the 95.5 percent allotment release rate posted in the same period under the 2025 General Appropriations Act (GAA).
Of the total released under the 2026 GAA, P3.47 trillion went to government departments, with a release rate of 94.5 percent of the adjusted P3.67-trillion programmed budget.

Among major agencies that had relatively lower release rates of their programs are the Department of Agriculture (DA) and Department of Tourism (DOT), which received below 90 percent of their program as of end-August.
The DA had only 68.8 percent of its P163.26-billion budget, slower than the 96.7 percent release rate posted a year ago.
Meanwhile, the DOT had P4.05 billion, or 87.4 percent, of its P4.64-billion adjusted program released.
The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) received 99.5 percent of its P530.12-billion budget as of end-August.
The Department of Education, which has the highest allocation in the national budget, received 92.5 percent of its record-high P961.14-billion budget, below last year’s 95.9-percent pace.
In terms of special purpose funds, the government has already released P518.52 billion, which is 72.1 percent of the adjusted P719.07-billion budget.
Automatic appropriations are at 89.9 percent or P2.16 trillion of the P2.4-trillion aggregate funding.
On the other hand, P120.11 billion was released for unprogrammed appropriations, particularly to support foreign-assisted projects.

Unprogrammed appropriations provide standby authority to incur additional agency obligations for priority programs or projects when revenue collection exceeds targets or when additional grants or foreign funds are generated.

The bulk of the unprogrammed appropriations, worth P80.15 billion, went to the Department of Transportation, P25.55 billion to DPWH, P13.88 billion to the Department of Social Welfare and Development, P511.03 million to Philippine Competition Commission and P23.79 million to the Department of Health.
PhilHealth budget

The government is proposing P74.45 billion for the Philippine Health Insurance Corp. (PhilHealth) in 2027, including P19 billion for improvements to benefit packages and other priority health interventions, according to the DBM.

The P19-billion funding is intended to support improvements in health benefits covering priority concerns such as mental health and severe malnutrition, as well as assistance involving hospitals operated by local government units (LGUs).

It will also cover the national government’s premium subsidies for qualified beneficiaries. About 11.09 million beneficiaries are targeted to receive the subsidies in 2027, up from around 10.65 million in 2026.
The proposed funding comes as the government implements measures intended to reduce patients’ out-of-pocket expenses for hospitalization.

In September, the DBM approved P10.377 billion for the implementation of the Zero Balance Billing (ZBB) program, including P9.377 billion for DOH hospitals nationwide and P1 billion for six pilot LGU hospitals in Benguet, Batangas, Laguna, Quezon, Aklan and Sarangani.
The DBM also released an additional P800 million to the Philippine General Hospital, specifically for ZBB.
DBM acting Secretary Kim Robert de Leon said government spending on health should result in direct assistance to patients.
“Every peso we release for health must ultimately reach the patient,” De Leon said in August.
He reiterated the point following the approval of the P10.377-billion ZBB funding.

“No Filipino should have to choose between obtaining the medical care they need and protecting their family from a hospital bill they cannot afford. This P10.377-billion release is intended to ensure that when our people become ill, the government is there to help shoulder the financial burden,” De Leon said.

The proposed PhilHealth allocation is part of the P353.8-billion health sector budget proposed for 2027. It also includes P107.29 billion for the operations of 72 DOH regional hospitals and other health facilities, P25.39 billion for the National Health Workforce Support System and P3.75 billion for the Cancer Assistance Fund.

PhilHealth received a total of P129.8 billion in government funding in 2026, following an initial P53.13-billion subsidy that was supplemented by P60 billion in funding recovery support and an additional P16.52 billion from the bicameral conference committee. – Christine Boton

articles.title: Escudero hits prosecutors for violating sub judice rule
articles.summary: Presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero yesterday issued show-cause orders against members of the House prosecution panel amid alleged violation of the sub judice ruling in the ongoing impeachment…

blocks.text: September 17, 2026 | 12:00am
Presiding officer Chiz Escudero made a lighthearted comment about private prosecutor Atty. Mae Divinagracia’s hoarse voice during the 18th day of the impeachment trial on August 25, 2026.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero yesterday issued show-cause orders against members of the House prosecution panel amid alleged violation of the sub judice ruling in the ongoing impeachment trial against Vice President Sara Duterte.
Escudero did not disclose the names of the members of the prosecution team who were included in the show cause orders.

Escudero has vowed the sub judice rule will be strictly enforced in Duterte’s impeachment trial as he has warned of public reprimand and admonition on the first offense and a P30,000 fine on the second.
He warned the prosecution – both the public and private panels – and the defense team that they could face contempt of court if they violated the sub judice rule.
Baste subpoenaed
Meanwhile, Escudero approved the issuance of a subpoena for Duterte’s brother, Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte.

“In regard to Mayor Sebastian Duterte… let the subpoena be issued only for Sept. 23. However, on Sept. 22, depending on where we are with respect to the three witnesses, we shall announce if we will be withdrawing that subpoena and simply issue a new one for the following week or the week thereafter. So as not to waste their time, given that they are all officials performing duties in connection with their functions,” Escudero said.
Defense spokesman Michael Poa said that it is the prerogative of the prosecution to request a subpoena for the mayor.

articles.title: Fluid vote threshold open to abuse – Azcuna
articles.summary: A changeable vote threshold can be easily manipulated by ruling political factions, retired Supreme Court associate justice Adolfo Azcuna warned yesterday, as he defended maintaining the required…

blocks.text: September 17, 2026 | 12:00am
Retired Supreme Court associate justice and former member of the Constitutional Commission Adolfo Azcuna.
STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — A changeable vote threshold can be easily manipulated by ruling political factions, retired Supreme Court associate justice Adolfo Azcuna warned yesterday, as he defended maintaining the required votes needed to convict an impeachable official at two-thirds of all 24 senators.

Responding to questions submitted by Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense counsel and read to the court by presiding officer Francis Escudero, the 1987 Constitution framer explained that basing the two-thirds threshold solely on actual attendance invites dangerous abuse.
“There is no guarantee. That’s the danger seen by the drafters of our Constitution. That’s why they made as basis or denominator the total membership of the Senate and Congress,” Azcuna said.
Asked if lowering the threshold could encourage a ruling administration to jail opposing lawmakers or deny them bail to skew numbers, Azcuna answered in the affirmative.

“There’s the danger of it getting abused by the president, not only the president, but even by members of the Senate, whoever controls the power of who can attend, who can prevent fellow members from attending… if you make the threshold dependent on actual attendance,” Azcuna said.

Retired chief justice Reynato Puno warned that any deliberate plot by a political faction to engineer absences and alter the voting base would render the trial unconstitutional. – Marc Jayson Cayabyab, Bella Cariaso

articles.title: Shock in Kosovo as Hague convicts former President Thaci
articles.summary: The conviction in The Hague of former President Hashim Thaci and three former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders has caused consternation in Kosovo — both among political leaders and on the streets. DW…

image.caption: A protester waves an Albanian flag outside the headquarters of the European Union Rule of Law Mission in Kosovo (EULEX) after former President Hashim Thaci was found guilty of war crimes by the Kosovo war crimes tribunal in The HagueImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS

blocks.text: The announcement of the verdict was greeted with shock and profound disappointment in Pristina.

Thousands of citizens had gathered in the main square of Kosovo's capital, many waving flags of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), to follow the announcement live on large screens. Similar gatherings took place across the country in Kosovo's main cities.

When it became clear that the Kosovo war crimes tribunal in The Hague had found former President Hashim Thaci guilty of war crimes — along with former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) leaders Kadri Veseli, Jakup Krasniqi and Rexhep Selimi — the crowd fell silent.
The silence was followed by calls for justice and chants of support for the four men.

Groups of citizens began trying to demolish sections of the perimeter wall surrounding EULEX, the EU Rule of Law Mission in Kosovo, which was deployed in Kosovo after the country's declaration of independence from Serbia in 2008 and continues to operate to this day.

blocks.caption: Thousands gathered in Pristina to watch the verdict from the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The HagueImage: Valdrin Xhemaj/REUTERS

blocks.text: Large numbers of Kosovo police officers and special units intervened to prevent further damage and incidents.
Political leaders in Kosovo respond
It wasn't just the people on the streets who were disappointed: Kosovo's political leaders were quick to respond to the news from The Hague.

"The conviction of the former KLA leaders is a terrible judgment for Kosovo, for our liberation war," said Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca, who was present in the courtroom in The Hague when the verdict was announced. He called it "a major blow to the state and to the domestic narrative."
"Kosovo experienced the war itself. We know what the KLA war was about, and we know that there was no criminal mechanism to harm any population. It is a sad, unjust and undeserved decision," he said.
Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti called the verdict an "unacceptable injustice."
"The conviction and such a severe sentence for four former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army is an unacceptable injustice, a great and harmful punishment," Kurti said on Wednesday.

The Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK), which was founded immediately after the war by Thaci and several other former KLA leaders, described the guilty verdict as an "unjust and unacceptable judgment," stressing that "the battle for justice continues until the very end."

"In The Hague, the right of our people, who fought for freedom, survival and liberation from the Serbian state regime that killed, expelled and terrorized Kosovo Albanians, was dealt a severe blow," the PDK said in a statement. "For us, this judgment represents a major injustice because it is based on allegations and material that we consider fabricated and which, over the years, have been promoted by the Serbian state apparatus and propaganda in an effort to criminalize the just war of the Kosovo Liberation Army."

The response from Kosovo's acting president, Albulena Haxhiu, was similar. She described the convictions of the four men as "a severe blow to their families, deeply shocking news for the Republic of Kosovo and a grave moment for the Albanian nation wherever it lives."

"On a day like this, the weight of this decision cannot be separated from the history from which we have emerged," Haxhiu wrote in her statement. "Kosovo experienced firsthand the violence of a state apparatus that killed civilians, committed massacres, expelled hundreds of thousands of Albanians from their homes and left behind thousands of people killed or missing. This experience is an indelible part of the memory of Kosovo and the Albanian nation."
Charges of crimes against humanity dismissed

The panel of judges at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague handed down the guilty verdicts over three years after the start of the trial and nearly six years after the four men were charged with war crimes and crimes against humanity during the 1998–99 Kosovo War.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Hashim Thaci listen to the announcement of the verdict against the former president and three other former KLA leaders Image: Valdrin Xhemaj/REUTERS

blocks.text: Though the three-judge panel dismissed the charges of crimes against humanity, the four men were convicted of war crimes against civilians and political opponents who did not support the KLA during the war.

Thaci, who was indicted while serving as president of Kosovo, was sentenced to 25 years in prison. Jakup Krasniqi, who served as a KLA spokesman and later as speaker of Kosovo's parliament on several occasions, was also sentenced to 25 years in prison. Kadri Veseli, who headed the KLA intelligence service during the war, was sentenced to 18 years in prison, and Rexhep Selimi, who served as chief inspector of the KLA military police, was sentenced to 13 years in prison.
Defense lawyers for the men said they would appeal the verdict.
The Kosovo Specialist Chambers

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers, which was set up by the Kosovo Assembly (parliament) in 2015, is staffed by international judges and based in The Hague. It deals exclusively with cases relating to allegations of crimes committed by members of the KLA during the Kosovo War.
Before returning to join Kosovo's struggle for independence in 1998, Thaci had been a student in Switzerland.

As a political leader of the former KLA, he received support from Western leaders, who invited him to participate in the 1999 peace talks in Rambouillet, France. At the time, Thaci was seen in Kosovo as a leader who could guide the country toward independence.

About 13,000 civilians — most of them Kosovo Albanians — were killed, and more than 1 million people were displaced during the war, which saw Kosovo, at the time a Serbian province, fighting for independence.

blocks.caption: Protesters also gathered outside the building that houses the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague after the verdict was announcedImage: Omar Havana/REUTERS

blocks.text: Following NATO's intervention against Serbian forces and their withdrawal from Kosovo, Thaci founded his own political party and came to power, first as Kosovo's prime minister and later as president.
In 2008, Kosovo declared independence from Serbia, a move rejected and still not recognized by Belgrade, Moscow and Beijing. Kosovo's statehood is, however, recognized by over 100 countries.
Relations between Kosovo and Serbia remain tense after over 15 years of negotiations between the countries, mediated by the European Union and supported by the United States.
Thaci, who, like the other three men, denied the charges against him, resigned as president of Kosovo in 2020 to face the charges and defend himself in The Hague.

articles.title: Michelin-starred Seoul restaurant fined for using ants as garnish
articles.summary: The owner of the acclaimed establishment avoids jail but is made to pay 15 million won (£8,144; $10,965).

blocks.text: A two Michelin-starred restaurant in Seoul has been fined for using ants as a dessert garnish.

The owner of Evett in the South Korean capital was fined 15 million won (£8,144; $10,965), while the company operating the restaurant was fined 10 million won for violating the Food Sanitation Act, local media report.
Ants are not among the 10 insect species approved for human consumption in the east Asian nation. The approved list includes grasshoppers, locusts and some silkworms.

Prosecutors had sought a one-year prison term for the restaurant's owner, as well as a 20 million won fine - but the judge took the owner admitting the charge and having no prior criminal record into account.

However, the judge is reported as saying that, as well as violating food standards, the presence of heavy metals exceeding standards was detected in the ants when they were tested, meaning the "culpability is not light".
The owner was said to have been unaware that providing ants in food was prohibited in South Korea, as they are used as food elsewhere.
Their use as a topping for sorbets at Evett came to light after the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety found online reviews accompanied by photographs.
It said the owner had sprinkled three to five ants on certain dishes to give them a "sour taste", over a period of nearly four years - amounting to approximately 49,000 ants used as a garnish.
Most of the ants were imported from the US, while some came from Thailand, the ministry said.
The owner had argued that they were used in a "small part" of the restaurant's 15-course menu and that diners were told they could opt for a non-ant alternative topping.

Ants are eaten and sometimes even valued as a delicacy in several Asian, African and Latin American cultures. Weaver ants and their eggs are used in Thai and Cambodian cooking, while in Colombia, queen ants are as prized as caviar.
The Michelin Guide considers a two-star establishment as one that does "excellent cooking" and is "worth a detour".

articles.title: Former French culture minister goes on trial on corruption charges
articles.summary: Rachida Dati accused of lobbying for carmaker Renault-Nissan when she was member of European parliament

blocks.text: Rachida Dati, a former French culture minister, has gone on trial in Paris on corruption charges linked to dealings with the Renault-Nissan carmaking group.

Dati, 60, is accused of illegal lobbying when she accepted €900,000 (£770,000) in lawyer’s fees from a Netherlands-based subsidiary of Renault-Nissan while she was a member of the European parliament. The court will have to decide what the money was for.

Dati’s legal team denied all corruption allegations, saying she worked “exclusively” as a lawyer for the Renault-Nissan subsidiary. French prosecutors argue that she was instead paid to lobby for the carmaking group, an activity that is banned for members of the European parliament. Prosecutors said there was a lack of evidence to show Dati had carried out legal work.
Dati was placed under investigation in 2019 on suspicion of illegally lobbying for Renault-Nissan between October 2009 and February 2013, when she was an MEP.

Dati is on trial with Carlos Ghosn, the disgraced former Renault-Nissan chief, who will be tried in absentia. Ghosn, 72, was detained in Japan in November 2018 amid allegations of financial misconduct in a separate case involving a plot to falsify records about his personal pay in order to enrich himself. He dodged trial in Japan after escaping to Lebanon in an audio equipment case. He has denied all wrongdoing in the Japan case as well as in the Dati case.

French prosecutors argue that a legal services contract signed in 2009 between Dati and Ghosn, in which Dati was paid an annual fee of €300,000, was used to disguise lobbying work. Investigators obtained the contract in 2019 during a search of Renault’s headquarters after Ghosn’s arrest in Japan.

Dati, 60, who is the district mayor of the 7th arrondissement in Paris, is one of the most prominent figures on the French right. She was the first woman of north African and Muslim heritage to hold a major French government post when she was appointed justice minister by the rightwing president Nicolas Sarkozy. She returned to government under Emmanuel Macron, as culture minister.

Dati redefined political celebrity in France, and has said growing up as the second of 11 children on a low-income housing estate on the outskirts of Chalon-sur-Saône in Burgundy gave her a greater understanding of the French electorate. She ran for mayor of Paris earlier this year, but lost to the Socialist Emmanuel Grégoire.
If convicted, Dati faces up to 10 years in prison and a fine of up to €450,000. She could also face a five-year ban on holding public office.
Dati’s lawyers said: “Unfounded allegations of influence peddling in the European parliament stem from an artificial intellectual construct devised by the prosecution.”
after newsletter promotion

In a separate investigation, Dati has been accused of accepting nearly €300,000 in undeclared payments from the energy group GDF Suez, also while an MEP. Prosecutors said last year they were looking into reports Dati failed to declare jewellery and watches worth €420,000 upon taking ministerial office.
She has denied any wrongdoing in all cases.

articles.title: Charlie Kirk's family alleges 'stunning failures' by Utah officials led to his assassination
articles.summary: The conservative activist was speaking to a crowd of thousands on the university campus when he was shot and killed by a gunman positioned on a roof.

blocks.text: Charlie Kirk's family has accused the Utah Valley University and state officials of "stunning failures and reckless decisions" that they say led to the conservative activist's 2025 assassination during a campus event.
In a legal notice, lawyers for the family say Kirk's Turning Point USA event at the university campus was not properly secured or monitored, making him an easy target.
Kirk, 31, was speaking to a crowd of thousands on the university campus, when he was shot and killed by a gunman positioned on a roof.
The university said it was aware of the claim but did not comment further on the allegations, according to a statement shared with the BBC's US partner CBS News.

"We are aware of the notice of claim. UVU addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes, " the university said in its statement. "Our focus remains on supporting our campus community."
The legal notice was filed on 9 September, a day ahead of the one-year anniversary of Kirk's death, and is typically a precursor to a lawsuit.
It names Utah Valley University, local police, the state of Utah, and other university officials as parties who were allegedly aware of the threats against Kirk and did not take steps to protect him.
"Through a series of stunning failures and reckless decisions, the UVU Parties created a foreseeable danger to Charlie," the notice alleges.

"Placing a politically controversial figure like Charlie Kirk in an outdoor event in the quad surrounded by tall buildings and other elevated observation platforms is accurately described as walking him into a fishbowl," it says.
Kirk's family alleges the university failed to conduct a meaningful security assessment ahead of the event, failed to assign enough police officers, and did not have an ambulance available on site.
The family also alleges the university ignored warnings about securing the rooftops surrounding the courtyard where Kirk was speaking.

"The risk of a rooftop shooter should have been especially top-of-mind given the attempted assassination of President Trump, Charlie Kirk's close friend and political ally, by a rooftop shooter the previous year," the family's attorney D Loren Washburn wrote in the court filing.
Tyler Robinson, a 23-year-old man from Utah, who has been accused of shooting Kirk from a roof, is due to appear in court next month to hear the date of his trial.
Robinson denies aggravated murder, a capital offence in the state, as well as six other charges.
Prosecutors have called for the death penalty.

articles.title: British-American writer Bonnie Greer dies aged 77
articles.summary: Chicago-born playwright Bonnie Greer, who became a familiar face in British political discourse later in life, has died. Her husband David Hutchins announced news of Greer's death.

image.caption: Chicago-born Greer moved to the UK in 1986 and acquired dual citizenship around a decade later [FILE: February 2020]Image: Mark Thomas/i Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Playwright and author Bonnie Greer died aged 77, her husband David Hutchins said on Wednesday in a statement to British media.
A celebrated writer born in Chicago who at first plied her trade in New York, Greer spent most of her adult life in the UK.
She took up dual citizenship and became a regular and prominent political commentator in Britain.

blocks.caption: Greer attended the Frankfurt book fair in 2019 at the height of the post-Brexit debate for a panel on the topicImage: DW/E. Grenier

blocks.text: What did Greer's husband say about her death?

Greer's widower Hutchins hailed her as "an acclaimed playwright, author, critic, cultural and political commentator whose intelligence, courage and distinctive voice made an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life."
Hutchins said his late wife had suffered succumbed to a brief illness.
He said those closest to Greer would remember her warmth, humor, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together.
"To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her," Hutchins said. The pair married in 1993, seven years after Greer emigrated.

blocks.caption: Greed became a prominent political commentator and activist in the UK [FILE: October 2017]Image: Jonathan Nicholson/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Who was Bonnie Greer?
Greer was born in Chicago in 1948, the eldest of seven children from a family of Mississippi sharecroppers.
Her familial exposure to the UK predated even her birth — her father Ben was stationed in Britain during World War II and had taken part in the D-Day landings.
She gravitated towards creative writing amid the civil rights movement in the US after a college professor told her he did not believe women should pursue a legal career.
Having studied theater in Chicago she moved to New York as a young aspiring writer.
Greer settled in the UK in 1986 and worked mainly in theater with women and ethnic minorities.

She acquired British citizenship in 1997 and wrote a series of successful radio plays aired on the BBC and musicals. Her 1993 play "Munda Negra" exploring mental health problems among black women won the Verity Bargate Award for best play.
Greer also became a frequent contributor to political and social debate in Britain, frequently appearing on topical shows like "Newsnight" and "Question Time".

Greer was a prominent supporter of Barack Obama and wrote a memoir and personal musical history in 2009 called "Obama Music." She also campaigned against the UK's exit from the EU, Brexit, and Donald Trump's first term as US president at around the same time.

She held a series of cultural roles, including being president of the Bronte Society, chancellor of Kingston upon Thames University in London, a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature, and a board member of the Royal Opera House and the London Film School.

articles.title: Gaza: At least 21 dead, including children, in building collapse
articles.summary: The search for survivors has been hampered by Israeli restrictions on heavy machinery in the Gaza Strip. Authorities say 2,000 damaged buildings in the territory are occupied by families who have…

image.caption: The search for survivors is ongoing but hampered by Israeli restrictions on heavy machineryImage: Mahmoud Issa/REUTERS

blocks.text: At least 21 people, including six children, were killed in the Gaza Strip in the early hours of Wednesday morning when a war-damaged building collapsed, injuring at least 14 more people and trapping dozens of others beneath the rubble.
On Wednesday, rescue workers were still searching through the wreckage — in many cases with their bare hands given the lack of heavy machinery in the devastated Palestinian enclave.

"We are still hearing voices from under the rubble," said Raed Al-Dahshan, the director of Gaza City's civil defense service, adding that at least 10 families had lived in the collapsed building and expressing hope that more survivors could yet be found.

"My friend and neighbors live in this building," resident Mohannad Al-Mashharawi told the AFP news agency. "I came to help my friend retrieve some clothes and mattresses. He currently has no shelter or home."
The death toll is expected to rise as the search for victims buried in the rubble continues.
Gaza: Hundreds of buildings at risk of collapse

"The situation, you see, is tragic because we don't have the equipment and machinery that is needed," said Alessandro Mrakic, head of the United Nations (UN) Development Program's Gaza office. "So there are actually people ​are digging with their bare hands."
With wetter autumn and winter weather approaching, Mrakic warned that rain water could destabilize hundreds of other bombed-out buildings in the war-torn territory.
"There are approximately 400 buildings at risk of collapse," he said. "And we know that these buildings will collapse, especially now with the upcoming winter."

According to authorities, about 2,000 damaged buildings in Gaza are still inhabited by Palestinian families, many of whom have told the Reuters news agency that it is the only way to shelter from the wind and rain in the absence of sufficient tents.

"Today's tragedy underscores the grave risks faced by families living in these structures and the urgent need for safer alternatives," said Ramiz Alakbarov, UN Humanitarian ⁠Coordinator for ​the Occupied Palestinian Territory.
"No one should have to risk their life simply to find a safe place to shelter."
Israeli restrictions on heavy machinery
Palestinian and UN officials have blamed Israel's restrictions on Gaza for the lack of heavy machinery available in the enclave.

Israel says it wants to keep such machines out of the hands of Hamas militants, who used such equipment in their deadly raid into Israel in October 2023, prompting Israel's devastating assault on Gaza which has since killed over 73,000 Palestinians — the vast majority of them civilians.

More than 1,300 Palestinians, also mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza since a US-backed ceasefire in October 2025, while the Israeli military says four of its soldiers soldiers have been killed.

articles.title: Forgotten US court of 'secrecy' could mean more deportations
articles.summary: The use of a secretive and long dormant court in the deportation of a woman from the US could have significant consequences. The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was just used for the first time in its…

image.caption: The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was used for the first time in three decades Image: Public Domain/U.S. Federal Government

blocks.text: An estimated 4.5 million people have been deported from the US since 1996. But until this month, not one of those cases had involved the Alien Terrorist Removal Court (ATRC).

Nazira Haji Zada, 47, from Afghanistan, lived in Texas and had legal US permanent residency. According to a statment released by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on Wednesday, she has now returned to Afghanistan after she "conceded she is an alien terrorist and waived appeal of the removal order, terminating her previous status."
"This landmark case, resulting in the prompt removal of this alien terrorist to her country of origin, is a win for national security and the rule of law," said US Attorney General Todd Blanche.
US Senate confirms Trump lawyer Blanche as attorney general
However, Zada's public defenders Matthew Farley and Mary Manning Petras earlier said that the case "should not be seen as an endorsement of this court’s legitimacy."

The court, founded as part of a raft of anti-terror measures after the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing, was set up to deal with non-US citizens facing terrorism-related charges on which the evidence is confidential or somehow related to national security.
ATRC never needed before

Hiroshi Motomura, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), told DW that it appears the Donald Trump administration is using the ATRC as the latest tool in its deportation toolkit.

"This is a very elaborate procedure. There are so many other ways that you can essentially get someone out of the United States by using the word terrorism in the context of removal proceedings," he said.
"From a very practical perspective, the government's non-use reflects its view over the last 30 years that 'we don't need this court because we can essentially deport people without it.'"

Zada was accused by prosecutors of being the "matriarch" of a family in which two men — son, Abdullah Haji Zada, and son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhed — had been found guilty of plotting to carry out a mass shooting on election day in 2024. Earlier this year, Blanche described the family as "ISIS-sympathizing."

For Motomura, who has written a number of books and teaches on immigration and citizenship, one of the key distinctions between the ATRC and regular means of deportation is that those on trial do not have a chance to view the evidence against them. Their lawyers may be able to in some cases.
Secrecy inherent in operation of ATRC

"I'm speculating, although I think not unreasonably, that this is someone against whom they cannot invoke terrorism or other grounds without the kind of disclosure in court that they would not want to have," Motomura said.
DHS said in the statement released on Wednesday that they provided Zada and her lawyers with "half a terabyte of documents," though it did not disclose what these showed.

"So they would rather go through a more elaborate procedure and disclose it in chambers to a judge as opposed to having it be potentially more public," Motomura said. "Because the procedure that this court provides is a procedure that calls for some disclosure, but also calls for some secrecy."
The ATRC consists of five federal trial court judges selected by the chief justice of the US Supreme Court, John Roberts, who was appointed by George W. Bush in 2005.

The government must first apply to the court demonstrating it has probable cause to suggest a person is an "alien terrorist" under the immigration law definition. It must also lay out why proceeding through standard deportation procedures would be a national security risk. In Zada's case this happened in July.

Then comes the hearing, in which the government need only prove their case "by the preponderance of the evidence", a lower bar than usually applied to such cases. Zada's decision to leave the country without the hearing means that the feasibility of the government using the court in future remains somewhat in the balance due to a constitutional point that was not tested.
Due process constitutional question yet to be resolved

"Dragging lawful permanent residents into court but refusing to show them or their attorneys the evidence that will be used against them is a plain violation of due process. We are confident that the Alien Terrorist Removal Court will be struck down as unconstitutional as soon as a judge is asked to address the issue," said Zada's lawyers in a statement to the Washington Post.

blocks.caption: US Attorney General Todd Blanche hailed the deportation as a "win for national security"Image: Rod Lamkey/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: An amendment to the US constitution states that no state can "deprive any person of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law." Whether this applies in cases such as Zada's is not yet clear, something Motomura said may frustrate the Trump administration.

"I bet they were disappointed. I don't know this, but it would not surprise me if they're disappointed that the case never got litigated in court on the constitutional issue because it would allow them a different opportunity to limit the rights of people in the United States under the US Constitution," he said.

Given the Trump administration's stated "zero tolerance" policy on immigration — which has also included deporting people to so-called ‘third countries' they have no connection with and the widespread deployment of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents — it seems likely it won't be 30 years before another case is brought before the ATRC. And that could have significant implications for justice.

"I think it's very hard to view this situation accurately without seeing it as part of a broader effort by the administration to limit access to courts and to legal counsel and access to evidence on multiple fronts," concluded Motomura.

articles.title: Allies, victims' families react to Rodrigo Duterte's first in-person ICC appearance
articles.summary: Allies of former President Rodrigo Duterte and families of victims of his administration"s war on drugs reacted to his first in-person appearance before the International Criminal Court on Wednesday.

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 11:03pm
Allies of former President Rodrigo Duterte and families of victims of his administration’s war on drugs reacted to his first in-person appearance before the International Criminal Court on Wednesday.
Dressed in a black suit and white shirt, Duterte attended the third status conference in his crimes against humanity case as part of preparations for his trial, which is set to begin on November 30.
Duterte was arrested and taken to The Hague on March 12, 2025. He last appeared before the ICC via video link on March 14, 2025.
On Facebook, Senator Robin Padilla posted photos of Duterte’s appearance before Trial Chamber III, captioned simply, “Tatay.”
Senator Christopher “Bong” Go, who served as Duterte’s aide for more than two decades, also posted images from the status conference, captioned, “Tatay Digong.”

“We’re happy that he has finally appeared and that he looks OK. In fact, he looks like he has put on weight,” said Llore Pasco, whose two sons were killed during Duterte’s war on drugs, as she watched a television broadcast of the hearing from Manila.

“When I saw Duterte’s face, I felt a sense of relief, knowing that he is still there in The Hague. He cannot leave. Thank you to the ICC for taking care of Duterte there for us so that we can achieve true justice,” said Sally Ramos, the mother of another drug war casualty, in a report by Raffy Tima on “24 Oras.”
In January, ICC judges said Duterte’s health was good enough for him to follow the proceedings and requested that he appear in court in person rather than via video link from the detention unit.

The warrant for Duterte’s arrest says he was responsible for a widespread and systematic campaign that led to thousands of killings between 2011 and 2019, including during his time as mayor of Davao City.
Police said 6,200 suspects were killed during anti-drug operations, but human rights groups said the actual number could be higher.

Duterte said he had instructed police to act in self-defense and told supporters he was ready to “rot in jail” if it meant ridding the Philippines of illicit drugs. —with a report from Reuters/VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Panganiban makes 'binata' quip as Hontiveros questions him
articles.summary: Retired Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban directed a flirtatious remark at Sen. Risa Hontiveros as the latter questioned him during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 11:02pm

Retired Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban on Wednesday directed a flirtatious remark at Senator Risa Hontiveros as the latter questioned him during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Panganiban was appearing at the Senate court as one of the four amici curiae invited to weigh in on the conviction threshold of the impeachment court.
During her questioning, Hontiveros said that Panganiban was free to answer questions she would be asking to the other experts.
Panganiban said that he would even entertain Hontiveros’ questions in private.

“Maski po sa pribado na conversation natin, pwede ako sumagot… dalaga naman po kayo,” the 88-year-old joked with a smile. (Even in private we can have a conversation, I can answer… after all, you are unmarried.)
Senate impeachment court Presiding Officer Chiz Escudero then jokingly asked Hontiveros: “Can you confirm?”
Hontiveros chose to laugh it off. "Ibang mga tanong pa po ang itatanong ko, Mr. Presiding Officer, sa ating mga amicus curiae," she said.
(I have other questions to ask the other amici curiae.)
“Di ko rin nasabi, binata rin ako,” Panganiban added, laughing. (I was not able to say it but I am a bachelor.)
“I’m sure marami po nagno-note niyan,” Hontiveros replied. (I’m sure plenty are taking note.)

Both Panganiban and Hontiveros are widowed. Panganiban lost his wife, Professor Elenita Carpio-Panganiban, in 2023 after 62 years of marriage, while Hontiveros, who lost her husband Francisco Baraquel Jr. in 2005, said she has a longtime partner. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: US officials decide against backing Saudi Arabia in Yemen after meeting Houthi leaders
articles.summary:
Armed group appears to reach agreement with Trump administration over safety of Red Sea shipping

Officials from the US met Houthi leaders over the weekend at the country’s embassy in Muscat,…

blocks.text: Officials from the US met Houthi leaders over the weekend at the country’s embassy in Muscat, Oman, it has been confirmed, leading to the US decision not to intervene to help Saudi Arabia drive back a Houthi advance inside Yemen.

The Houthis reassured the US that the ceasefire agreement between the two sides struck in 2025 still held and the movement had no intention of attacking US shipping in the Red Sea. Only Saudi-linked shipping was regarded as a target owing to its blockade of Yemen, the Houthis confirmed.

The meeting helps to explain the decision from the US president, Donald Trump, to condemn the Houthi advance down the west coast of Yemen for threatening freedom of navigation through the Bab al-Mandab strait, but so far to reject any military response in support of Riyadh. The US is already embroiled in an expensive and resource sapping conflict with Iran, which backs the Houthis.

The US labelled the Houthis as a foreign terrorist entity in March 2025, but in the recent past has met leaders from Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran. The US vice-president JD Vance confirmed on Monday that the US was in direct contact with the Houthis.

The US refusal to become directly involved has put pressure on Saudi Arabia to reach either a diplomatic solution with the Houthis over the future governance of Yemen, or to try to build a regional alliance with Pakistan and Turkey to force the Houthis back. In a lightning offensive last week, the Houthis seized control of large swathes of western Yemen along the Red Sea coast.

The former deputy US ambassador to Yemen, Nabeel Khoury, said a “kind of tacit understanding between the Trump administration and the Houthis” had been struck. Khoury added: “The Houthis are promising the American administration that American and international navigation will not be affected in the Red Sea, but the only danger is to Saudi ships or those carrying Saudi oil.”

In a bid to build popular support against the Houthis in the region, Riyadh made the controversial claim that the Houthis had fired a drone at the holy city of Mecca on Tuesday, but the missile had been destroyed by Saudi defence forces. It said the drone was entering a prohibited airspace close to Mecca’s most holy shrines. The drone was intercepted at about 6.50pm local time on Tuesday, coalition spokesperson Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki said in a statement.

Saudi Arabia said any attack on Mecca is a red line and the move was condemned in lengthy statements by the UN-recognised Yemen government based in Aden as well as the 57-country Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. The Pakistani prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, condemned what he described as a “dastardly and heinous” attempted attack on Mecca. “The people of Pakistan are saddened and perturbed by this outrageous act,” he said in a statement posted on X.

Houthi leadership – followers of a Shia Zaydism that respects the pilgrimage to Mecca – dismissed the claim as the lie of the century, adding that such worn-out lies had been used before and had fooled no one.

The Houthi’s deputy foreign minister, Abdul Wahid Abu Ras, said “whoever opened the land of the two holy mosques to debauchery and entertainment parties, and whoever defiled the land of the two holy mosques by the presence of Zionist Jews in it, is the one who targets Mecca, Medina and the Islamic holy sites”.

The Houthis countered that they had shot down a Saudi F-15 plane close to Marib, and attacked an Aramco plant in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu. No supporting evidence was provided by the Houthi military spokesperson, but the head of the Houthi negotiating team, Mohammed Abdul Salam, said the downing of the plane was a warning to the west not to fall victim to Saudi propaganda.

Mohammed al-Farah, a Houthi political bureau member, said: “The truth is that Saudi Arabia is experiencing a real predicament in Yemen. It became embroiled in a war, a siege and an occupation, and then failed to achieve its goals.

“Today, it is looking for external solutions, so it is begging the international community, warning the world about Bab al-Mandab and requesting support from Pakistan, Turkey, America, Israel and Egypt. Then it is trying to mobilise Muslims with a false pretext called ‘targeting Mecca’.”

Separately, Israeli officials have leaked details of a secret meeting between military commanders from the US, Israel and several Arab states in Germany last week to discuss the war launched by Israel and the US against Iran. The report from Axios journalist Barak Ravid said the “private retreat” was organised by the commander of US Central Command (Centcom), Adm Brad Cooper.
after newsletter promotion

Citing two unnamed Israeli officials, Ravid reported that the meeting was attended by the military chiefs of staff of Israel, Saudi Arabia the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar Jordan and Egypt. It was the first such gathering since the US and Israel went to war with Iran more than six months ago. Israel, once a target for the Houthis, is offering to intervene in Yemen on Saudi Arabia’s behalf.

A meeting of the UN security council on Tuesday condemned any attempt to close the Red Sea, but the meeting was notable for the Russian envoy beginning to edge away from its previous stance that the UN-recognised government based in Aden was the only legitimate government inside the country.

In Beijing, the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, on Wednesday met his Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi, in a bid to secure Chinese support for its plans for the future administration of the strait of Hormuz. The strait remains effectively closed owing to separate Iranian and US blockades.

A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said China does not want to see further regional tension spill over into Yemen and the Red Sea. The Chinese called on the US to return to the talks based on the memorandum of understanding agreed between the two sides in June. Beijing, the main importer of Iranian oil, is eager for a settlement and is resisting any suggestion that US secondary sanctions applied to countries trading with Iran should apply to its own country.
Oil prices remain well over $100 (£74) a barrel and a key Saudi East-West pipeline remains closed because of a bombing incident.

articles.title: St. John's woman with 160 prior convictions, including for fraud and forgery, gets jail time in CERB case
articles.summary: After several trial delays, former housing advocate Michelle Voisey is headed back to prison after pleading guilty to fraud.

image.caption: Michelle Voisey, seen here in a file photo, has been sentenced to 10 months in jail for using her niece's CRA account to send herself $8,000 in CERB payments. (Mark Cumby/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New
After several trial delays, former housing advocate Michelle Voisey is headed back to prison after pleading guilty to fraud.
Michelle Voisey has been handed a 10-month jail sentence
A former St. John’s housing advocate is returning to jail for the latest in a long list of criminal convictions.

Michelle Voisey was handed a 10-month sentence with 24 months probation for using her niece’s Canada Revenue Agency account to send $8,000 worth of Canada Emergency Response Benefit payments to her own bank account.
The federal program, known as CERB, provided financial support to people who lost their jobs during the COVID-19 pandemic.

items: St. John's housing advocate pleads guilty to fraud, but legal aid request delays sentencing
Sentencing of St. John's serial fraudster and former housing advocate delayed again

blocks.text: “The seriousness of the offence lies not only within the amount taken, but also its deliberate nature, the abuse of trust, the impact on the victim and Ms. Voisey’s extensive history of similar offending,” Justice Peter Browne said at Voisey’s sentencing hearing in Supreme Court in St. John's on Sept. 11.
Former St. John’s housing advocate gets jail sentence for fraud

Browne ordered Voisey to repay the $8,000 to CRA, and banned her from holding any job or volunteer position where she would have authority over another person's property or money for a period of 20 years.

Browne said Voisey’s decision to plead guilty was a mitigating factor in his decision, though he also considered her criminal history. Voisey has nearly 160 previous convictions, many involving fraud, forgery or theft.
“This record demonstrates a long standing and deeply entrenched pattern of dishonest conduct,” Browne said.
Voisey charged back in 2021

According to the statement of facts, Voisey's niece contacted police when her GST payment didn't arrive on time. She learned that $8,000 in CERB payments had been paid out in her name — even though she hadn't applied and didn't qualify for the benefit. Voisey was charged in October 2021.

In 2023, while the case was winding its way through court, Voisey, operating under the name Michelle Gushue, participated in the tent city protest on Confederation Hill. Voisey participated in media interviews and solicited donations of gift cards, cell phones, cash and more through social media.
Voisey’s latest conviction is unrelated to the tent city protest.
Voisey pleaded guilty in June 2025, but a last-minute request for a legal aid lawyer delayed sentencing until 2026.

items: St. John's housing advocate pleads guilty to fraud, but legal aid request delays sentencing
Sentencing of St. John's serial fraudster and former housing advocate delayed again

blocks.text: At Friday’s sentencing, Voisey’s lawyer, Dan Furey, submitted a letter he said is from her family doctor, indicating that she's been diagnosed with ovarian cancer. Browne declined to take the letter into consideration in sentencing, explaining that the defence would need to make an oral application and call in an expert witness, like an oncologist.
“I'm not prepared to entertain any of that without expert evidence and in this courtroom to know if incarceration would affect any type of [...] treatment,” he said.

Furey declined to make the application and the sentencing proceeded. After the sentence was handed down, Voisey asked if she could still make the application, but Browne said no. She asked for her sentence to be delayed for two days, but Browne denied that request too.
CBC News has asked Furey if Voisey intends to appeal her sentence.
